📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that exploring non-stimulant ADHD treatment? Use these questions to guide your next doctor discussion.

Sources indicate that navigating Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) treatment options as an adult can feel overwhelming, but finding a treatment plan that aligns with your specific health goals is an notable first step. ADHD treatment isn’t one-size-fits-all. Non-stimulant treatments offer an option without controlled-substance management.

In a recent development, finding a treatment is a collaborative process. My role as a healthcare provider is to provide education and guidance to help patients make informed decisions about their care. As you explore whether non-stimulant options are the right fit for your daily routine, having clear, open communication is essential. To help guide a thoughtful, personalized conversation at your next doctor’s appointment, I’ve put together a list of key questions to help you get started. Dr. Jo Hughes is a paid consultant compensated by Supernus.

Non-stimulants are noncontrolled prescription medications used to treat the core ADHD symptoms, inattention, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity.

With consistent daily dosing, non-stimulant medications can provide continuous medication exposure over a 24-hour period.

Most non-stimulant medications offer a distinct and targeted approach to help manage daily ADHD symptoms, working gradually over time to improve symptom control.

Every non-stimulant ADHD medication has a different safety profile, so side effects can vary. Having an open conversation with your provider before starting treatment is the best way to ensure your blueprint fits your needs and daily routine.

Industry observers note that non-stimulants are noncontrolled medications. Talk to your doctor about prescription and refill options, including whether telehealth appointments are appropriate for you.

Sources indicate that qelbree® (viloxazine extended-release capsules) is a convenient once-a-day non-stimulant ADHD medication for adults and kids ages 6 years and older. It was the first non-stimulant ADHD medication approved in over a decade with approximately 3 million prescriptions filled since launch in 2021 (for children 6-17 years old) and 2022 (in adults 18 years and older).

Qelbree® (viloxazine extended-release capsules) is a prescription medicine used to treat ADHD in adults and children 6 years and older. Please click here for full Prescribing Information, including Boxed Warning, and Medication Guide.

In a recent development, qelbree may increase suicidal thoughts and actions in children and adults with ADHD, especially within the first few months of treatment or when the dose is changed. Tell your doctor if you or your child have (or if there is a family history of) suicidal thoughts or actions before starting Qelbree. Monitor your or your child’s moods, behaviors, thoughts, and feelings during treatment with Qelbree. Report any newly introduced or sudden changes in these symptoms right away.

See below for full Key Safety Information.

Beyond its established presence, Qelbree offers treatment versatility for patients with ADHD in a number of ways:.

Finding an ADHD treatment can take time, there isn’t a one-size-fits all approach. Schedule time with your doctor to discuss all your options, including if Qelbree may be a good fit for you.

To learn more, visit https://www.qelbree.com.

ADDitude does not endorse any specific product, service, or treatment.

Qelbree (viloxazine extended-release capsules) is a prescription medicine used to treat ADHD in adults and children 6 years and older.

Recent findings suggest that qelbree may increase suicidal thoughts and actions, in children and adults with ADHD, especially within the first few months of treatment or when the dose is changed. Tell your doctor if you or your child have (or if there is a family history of) suicidal thoughts or actions before starting Qelbree. Monitor your or your child’s moods, behaviors, thoughts, and feelings during treatment with Qelbree. Report any upcoming or sudden changes in these symptoms right away.

In a recent development, you should not take Qelbree if you or your child: Take a medicine for depression called a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) or have stopped taking an MAOI in the past 14 days. Also, you or your child should avoid alosetron, duloxetine, ramelteon, tasimelteon, tizanidine, and theophylline.

Sources indicate that qelbree can increase blood pressure and heart rate. Your or your child’s doctor will monitor these vital signs.

According to recent reports, qelbree may cause manic episodes in patients with bipolar disorder. Tell your doctor if you or your child show any signs of mania.

Recent findings suggest that do not drive or operate heavy machinery until you know how Qelbree will affect you or your child. Qelbree may cause you or your child to feel sleepy or tired.

Sources indicate that the most common side effects of Qelbree in patients 6 to 17 years are sleepiness, not feeling hungry, feeling tired, nausea, vomiting, trouble sleeping, and irritability, and in adults, insomnia, headache, sleepiness, tiredness, nausea, decreased appetite, dry mouth, and constipation. These are not all the possible side effects of Qelbree.

You are encouraged to report negative side effects of prescription drugs to the FDA.

Visit www.fda.gov/medwatch or call 1-800-FDA-1088.

Please see Medication Guide, including Boxed Warning.

25 unique experience gift ideas for everyone on your list

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Maybe you’ve had the experience where you’ve opened a gift that didn’t quite land… Another candle, another kitchen gadget, another book you probably won’t read.
  • According to recent reports, when life can feel increasingly materialistic, receiving the gift of an experience can feel like an extra special treat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Maybe you’ve had the experience where you’ve opened a gift that didn’t quite land… Another candle, another kitchen gadget, another book you probably won’t read.

According to recent reports, when life can feel increasingly materialistic, receiving the gift of an experience can feel like an extra special treat. A coffee date, a class you could take together, or a simple invitation to step away from your routine for a few hours. Gifting experiences is becoming more common as people increasingly value things to do rather than things to have. Experiences create memories, prolonged joy, and ways to connect and bond with your loved ones.

Let’s explore why this trend is becoming a thoughtful option for many, and how to choose the right option for the people in your life.

In a recent development, gifting an experience means offering someone the chance to do or enjoy something, rather than giving them a physical item. It could be a short outing, a shared class, a small adventure, or even a moment of relaxation. The focus is on creating a meaningful interaction or memory.

According to recent reports, at its core, an experience gift acknowledges who someone is and what matters to them — comfort, curiosity, connection, or rest. It’s a way of saying, I see what brings you joy or ease, and building a shared experience around that. This can feel especially supportive for people whose lives are busy or emotionally stretched.

Industry observers note that because these gifts are flexible, they work across relationships and budgets. They can be shared or solo, active or restful, planned or open-ended. They offer a moment that feels nourishing and special for someone you care about.

💙 If relaxation is what they need, a Calm gift card gives them access to sleep support, meditation, and stress tools.

While research on experience gifting is still growing, studies highlight how shared time and supportive interactions can strengthen relationships and help people feel more connected.

It has been revealed that and for the giver, choosing an experience can relieve some of the pressure to pick the “perfect” item. Plus, you get to be a bit more creative since experiences can be catered to the person in question more accurately than a fresh sweater or scented bath salts.

In a recent development, these gifts also tend to linger in memory. A walk through a latest neighborhood, a class where you learned something together, or an afternoon spent doing something familiar but intentional can shape how people feel long after the moment ends. The emotional takeaway is often stronger than anything wrapped.

Choosing an experience gift doesn’t need to feel complicated. A few gentle questions can help you find something that feels both thoughtful and doable:.

What feels realistic for them right now?

What genuinely matches their interests?

Will this support connection in a way that feels natural?

Industry observers note that these considerations keep the focus on care rather than wow-factor. The most memorable experience gifts are often the ones that feel easy to say yes to.

Related read: What is the receiving gifts love language? Plus, 10 examples.

It has been revealed that experience gifts don’t have to be big, expensive, or Instagram-ready. The most meaningful ones usually feel simple, personal, and easy to follow through on. Below are ideas for different people in your life, with concrete examples and small tweaks to make each one feel low-pressure yet purposeful.

It has been revealed that 1. Slow morning together: Gift a “no-alarm morning” where you plan nothing except being together. This could look like making breakfast at home, wandering to a café, or staying in pajamas with a movie. You can write it as a simple coupon: “One slow morning: no chores, no intends, just us.” This works well for tired partners who crave rest more than busy plans.

2. A shared learning experience: Choose a class or workshop that feels fun. Cooking, pottery, a dance class, a cocktail-making session, or even a virtual class from home. The goal is to play, not create a upcoming skill. Pick a time that fits your usual schedule, and make it clear there’s no pressure to be good at it. You’re just trying it out.

Sources indicate that 3. A “memory lane” date: Revisit places that matter to your relationship: where you met, a favorite early date spot, or a park you love. You can build a simple route and add tiny prompts, like sharing a favorite memory at each stop. This turns a regular outing into something personal without costing much.

4. At-home retreat night: Create a mini retreat without leaving the house. That might mean takeout, candles, phones off for a few hours, and a shared activity like a puzzle, show, or playlist swap. You can include options on a card so they can choose: a massage, a movie, a board game, or just some quiet time together.

It has been revealed that 5. Surprise “care afternoon”: Block off a few hours for them where you take on a task they’ve been dreading—organizing a small space, handling an errand, or taking something off their mental load—and then follow it with something relaxing, like a walk or coffee. The experience is both practical support and quality time.

It has been revealed that 6. Future adventure fund: If money is tight or schedules are messy, create a “future adventure” envelope. Add a small amount of money, a short list of possible outings (day trip, concert, special restaurant), and a promise to choose an option together when life settles a bit. The gift is the intention and shared planning, not just the event itself.

Related read: How to build emotional connection in relationships.

1. Family game or movie night: Plan a night with a few easy games or a movie everyone can enjoy. Add snacks, cozy blankets, and a pause on chores for a few hours. You can give the night a “ticket” and let family members vote on the game or film. Keep it simple so no one has to host a perfect event.

2. Seasonal outing: Choose something tied to the time of year: apple picking, a beach afternoon, a holiday light walk, or a picnic in the park. The key is to keep expectations reasonable. Pick something close by, flexible with the weather, and not too long. Add a warm drink stop or simple treat to make it feel special.

In a recent development, 3. Family photo walk: Go for a walk through a neighborhood, park, or favorite spot and take casual photos of each other and everyday moments. This isn’t about staged portraits. It’s about capturing small, real pieces of your life together. Later, you can print a few favorites as a follow-up surprise.

4. Shared creative project: Start something you can all contribute to: a family recipe book, a small garden, a scrapbook, or a shared playlist for car rides. The “gift” is the first session to begin the project, plus a blueprint to keep it going at a relaxed pace.

5. Story or memory night: For older family members, gift a relaxed evening where you ask about their stories — childhood, early jobs, favorite memories. You can record audio or write things down if they’re comfortable. This can feel especially meaningful for grandparents or relatives who don’t often get to share their history.

6. Chore-free experience swap: Offer to trade time: you handle childcare, yard work, or a substantial errand so another family member can enjoy their own experience like a class, a nap, a solo walk, or quiet time at a café. The experience you’re gifting is space and freedom, which many busy adults crave more than objects.

In a recent development, 1. Friendship field trip: Pick a spot you’ve both wanted to visit, maybe a new café, nearby town, market, bookstore, or trail. Make it simple: transportation, one planned stop, and room to wander. You can name it something fun on the card, like “Field Trip Day: You + Me + Snacks.”.

2. Theme night at home: Instead of going out, bring the theme to your living room. Taco night, cozy soup night, DIY spa night, or favorite childhood snacks night. The gift is that you proposal the details so your friend just shows up and relaxes. This works well for introverts or friends on a budget.

In a recent development, 3. Shared creative time: Gift a “creative hang” where you both bring whatever you want to work on like, drawing, writing, knitting, music, or even organizing photos. Add music, snacks, and low-pressure conversation. For friends who feel guilty about not making time for hobbies, this can feel like a gentle permission slip.

Recent findings suggest that 4. Local class or workshop together: Check out low-stakes options like pottery, candle making, painting, or a casual fitness class. Pick something that doesn’t require special gear or skills and frame it as an experiment, not a performance: “We’ll probably be bad at this, and that’s half the fun.”.

5. Walk-and-talk ritual: Offer a series of scheduled or flexible walk-and-talks. Maybe once a month, every other week, or whenever you both can manage. The experience is regular emotional check-ins built into movement and fresh air. If walking isn’t accessible, this can be a sit-and-sip ritual at a park or café.

Related read: How to be a better friend: 7 tips to improve your relationships.

In a recent development, 1. One-on-one “date” with you: Plan a simple outing centered around their interests like ice cream, a playground, a comic shop, the library, or a favorite café. The important part is your undivided attention — no multitasking, no rushing. You can make a small “VIP pass” with their name and the activity.

2. Activity day pass: Gift a trip to a kid-friendly place: zoo, aquarium, children’s museum, climbing gym, trampoline park, or mini golf. To keep expectations realistic, include what’s covered (entry, one snack) and how long you’ll stay. That clarity helps avoid meltdowns.

It has been revealed that 4. Backyard or park adventure: Create a small “explorer kit” experience. Maybe that’s a printed map, a simple scavenger hunt, or nature bingo. Then take them to a nearby park or backyard to complete it together. The kit can be as simple as a folded paper with things to look for: birds, leaves, colors, shapes.

It has been revealed that 5. Choose-your-own-activity coupon book: Instead of one substantial outing, make a few small coupons they can redeem over time: “Stay up 30 minutes late,” “Pick tonight’s dinner,” “Board game together,” “Extra story at bedtime.” This spreads the experience out and gives them a sense of choice.

6. Screen-time with purpose: If screens are part of your life (for most families, they are), turn it into an intentional experience. A planned movie night with popcorn and cozy blankets, or a co-op video game session where you play alongside them. The shift is from “background screen” to “shared screen time.”.

Recent findings suggest that 7. Skill-building mini lesson: Offer to teach them something they’ve shown interest in, like basic cooking, drawing, sewing, photography, or music. Keep it short and fun — 30 to 60 minutes with lots of breaks. The experience is meant to help them feel capable and supported, not pushed to master something.

Related read: 61 fun and simple mindfulness activities for kids to enjoy.

Good experience gifts feel easy to enjoy and don’t add pressure. Simple outings like a coffee date, museum visit, or nature walk work well, as do classes or small day trips.

If you’re unsure, think about what the person already loves—quiet spaces, creativity, movement, or social time—and choose something that gently supports those interests.

Industry observers note that budget-friendly experience gifts often center on time or support rather than cost. A homemade coupon for help with errands, a movie night at home, or a walk together can feel more meaningful than anything store-bought.

You can also offer a few options, like a baked treat, a playlist walk, or a shared hour of connection, so the gift feels personal without being expensive.

According to recent reports, experience gifts ease the pressure of traditional gifting and help strengthen connections. They don’t create clutter and often require less guesswork than choosing an item.

Because they create memories, they can feel more lasting and emotionally meaningful. Early research also suggests shared time and supportive interactions may help people feel more connected.

Examples include classes, tours, local events, shared meals, creative workshops, or simple nature outings. They can also be quieter moments like helping with a task or planning a cozy night in.

Even small gestures—like sharing a playlist—count. The impact comes from the feeling the experience creates, not the size of the activity.

Industry observers note that if you’re unsure, offer a few choices rather than picking one activity. Options like a coffee outing, nature walk, or game night let the person choose what fits their energy. A flexible gift card to a café, movie theater, or class platform also works. Choice keeps the gift from feeling like an obligation.

Industry observers note that families often enjoy simple, low-pressure activities that include everyone. Seasonal outings, game nights, and local events work well because they’re easy to proposal.

In a recent development, shared projects—like cooking or gardening—or gifts of time, such as taking on chores so someone can rest, can also be meaningful. The best family gifts support connection without adding stress.

Recent findings suggest that friends tend to appreciate experiences that feel connecting and relaxed. This might be a field trip to a new café, a creative class, a cozy night in, or a shared walk.

Some friends enjoy active outings, while others prefer crafting or volunteering together. The goal is to match their energy and make time together feel restorative.

In a recent development, experience gifts can feel better for some people because they avoid clutter, reduce pressure, and often feel more meaningful. They shift the focus toward presence and memory-making rather than buying things.

While not everyone prefers experiences, they offer a gentle alternative for people who value connection or feel overwhelmed by physical items.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When procrastination stems from anxiety or fear of failure, use this playbook to help your child get unstuck.

Here’s a familiar scenario: Your student with ADHD sits at the kitchen table, supposedly doing homework. Twenty minutes go by, and you check on their status. Nothing has been accomplished.

According to recent reports, in these moments, your child is invisibly, involuntarily grappling with the Wall of Awful, a term I coined to describe the emotional barrier people confront when faced with draining and/or daunting tasks (homework is a good example). Before your child can engage in work, they must get past this wall of emotions.

Many parents misinterpret the early warning signs of the Wall. They mistake difficulty starting a task for resistance or defiance. So they double down on being a taskmaster, or, alternatively, they hover and provide too much help. Neither tactic aids their child in the long run.

[Get This Free Download: What Are Your Teen’s Weakest Executive Functions?].

Instead, I recommend talking about the idea of a Wall of Awful that stands between students and certain tasks. Then, when red flags appear, the Wall becomes the problem, not the kid, enabling the parent and child to problem-solve together.

It has been revealed that the Wall of Awful can affect anyone, but kids with ADHD are especially susceptible because their weak executive functioning skills make completing tasks harder. These struggles, combined with previous failures or fears of failure, add extra emotional bricks to the Wall.

Here is a quick-start approach that parents can follow to help their student vault the Wall of Awful:.

12 common physical symptoms of anxiety (and how to ease them)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Anxiety doesn’t only impact your brain.
  • This is what the physical symptoms of anxiety feel like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Anxiety doesn’t only impact your brain. Sometimes the first sign is your heart pounding for no clear reason, or a wave of nausea before a substantial conversation. You might feel dizzy, short of breath, or like there’s a knot in your stomach. You’re not in immediate danger, but your body is reacting as if you are.

This is what the physical symptoms of anxiety feel like. They can be alarming, especially if you don’t recognize them as anxiety right away. But your body responds this way for a reason, and understanding it can take some of the fear out of the experience.

Below we’ll look at the most common physical symptoms of anxiety, why they happen, and some ways to ease them.

It has been revealed that anxiety can affect your body before you've consciously registered that you're anxious at all. These are among the most common physical symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Racing or pounding heart (palpitations): A fast-beating or fluttering heart is one of the most recognized signs of anxiety. When your body senses a threat, it releases adrenaline, which speeds up your heart rate to pump blood to your muscles faster. This is useful when you actually need to run. Less so when you’re just checking your inbox.

According to recent reports, 2. Shortness of breath: Anxiety can make you feel like you can’t get a full breath, or like you’re slightly suffocating. Anxious breathing tends to be shallow and fast, which can lower carbon dioxide levels in the blood. This can feel scary, and anxiety is a common cause.

3. Chest tightness or pain: Muscle tension is a core part of the anxiety response and can be most noticeable in your chest, where you might feel tightness, pressure, or even mild pain. Seek emergency care if you feel sudden or severe chest pain, pain with shortness of breath or sweating, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw.

4. Dizziness or lightheadedness: Fast, shallow breathing can also leave you feeling faint or spaced out.

5. Tingling or numbness: Lower carbon dioxide levels in the blood can affect nerve signals and cause tingling or a pins-and-needles feeling in the hands, feet, or face. It can feel unsettling, but it’s usually short-lived. Numbness on one side of the body, sudden weakness, or trouble speaking needs urgent care.

6. Sweating: Sweating is part of the fight-flight-freeze-fawn response. Anxiety and stress can switch on your sweat glands even when you’re not hot, especially on your palms, underarms, and face.

7. Nausea or upset stomach: Your gut and brain are closely connected through the vagus nerve. When anxiety activates the stress response, digestion can slow or become disrupted. That can cause stomach upset, nausea, cramping, or an urgent need to use the bathroom.

According to recent reports, 8. Dry mouth: The stress response can slow saliva production, so many people notice a dry or sticky mouth when they’re anxious. It’s common and usually temporary, though it can make speaking feel harder than usual.

It has been revealed that 9. Muscle tension, aching, or trembling: Anxiety hormones prime your muscles to act quickly. Sustained tension without a chance to release can cause aching, stiffness, or subtle trembling, particularly in the hands, legs, or jaw.

Recent findings suggest that 10. Headaches: Tension headaches often appear with anxiety and stress. They’re typically felt as a band of pressure around your head or tension in the neck and shoulders.

11. Difficulty sleeping: Anxiety and sleep tend to make each other worse. Anxious thoughts and a body that’s physically on alert make it hard to fall or stay asleep. Poor sleep, in turn, can heighten anxiety the next day, which is how the cycle keeps going.

12. Fatigue: Anxiety takes energy because running the stress response tires the body, and poor sleep or constant tension can add to it. Ongoing anxiety can leave people feeling exhausted even without much physical effort.

Industry observers note that note: Some of the above symptoms can also point to a medical condition. If you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or symptoms that are fresh, severe, or don’t feel like your usual anxiety, it’s best to seek medical care.

Anxiety triggers the fight-flight-freeze-fawn response (also known as the stress response). When your brain senses a threat, it activates the sympathetic nervous system and releases hormones like adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones prepare your body to respond to danger. Your heart rate increases, your breathing quickens, your muscles tense, and non-essential systems like digestion temporarily slow down.

According to recent reports, this response is useful when the threat is physical. The challenge is that your nervous system doesn’t always tell the difference between real danger and everyday stress. A tense conversation can trigger a milder version of fight-or-flight. The result is a body primed for action in situations that don’t call for it.

It has been revealed that for most people these symptoms rise and fall with the stressful moment. When anxiety is ongoing, the symptoms can stick around longer.

There’s no instant off switch for anxiety, but these approaches can help ease physical symptoms, both in the moment and over time.

Controlled breathing can help calm the nervous system, and research suggests slow breathing helps many people feel calmer. Slow, gentle breathing, especially with a longer exhale, can shift your body toward the rest-and-digest (parasympathetic) system, which counteracts the stress response.

Try: Breathe in through your nose for four counts and out slowly for six. Repeat for a few minutes. You could also try box breathing, where you rhythmically hold your breath between inhales and exhales.

💙 When your body needs help slowing down, we have a short, breath-focused session for you: Breathe to Calm Down with Chibs Okereke.

It has been revealed that grounding techniques can help pull your attention out of anxious thoughts and back to the present moment. The 5–4–3–2–1 technique is a popular choice. To try it, notice:.

💙 If anxiety is pulling you out of your body, try Tamara Levitt's Grounding session on Calm, which guides you back to solid earth.

Exercise is well-known for easing tension, and you might find that even a short walk can take the edge off. Science agrees, with research suggesting regular exercise can help reduce anxiety symptoms over time.

💙 Not sure where to start? Try this Mindful Movement session with Mel Mah on Calm to bring gentle, non-judgmental awareness to your body as it moves.

It has been revealed that progressive muscle relaxation involves intentionally tensing and releasing muscle groups throughout the body. It’s designed to help you relax by encouraging each muscle to unclench. It doesn’t take long, with typical sessions lasting just 10 to 20 minutes.

Try: Start with your feet. Tense the muscles for five seconds, then release completely. Work your way up through your calves, thighs, abdomen, hands, arms, shoulders, and face. Skip tensing any area that’s injured or painful.

💙 Not keen on the tensing? This guided Body Scan Meditation moves your attention gently through the body, one area at a time, no clenching required.

Mindfulness practices train your attention to rest on the present moment rather than looping through worries about what might happen.

Mindfulness is something you build with regular practice. Over time, it can lower how strongly your body reacts to stress, which means the physical symptoms of anxiety may appear less often, or feel less intense when they do.

💙 Work through Calm’s Letting Go of Anxiety series, which is designed to help you sit with anxious feelings instead of spiraling.

Caffeine is a stimulant that can raise your heart rate and cause jitteriness, which may feel like anxiety or make it stronger.

Alcohol may feel calming at first, but it can disrupt your sleep and may make anxiety worse.

Cutting back on both is worth considering if you’re dealing with anxiety symptoms frequently.

If physical symptoms of anxiety are frequent, severe, or getting in the way of daily life, talking with a doctor or mental health professional is a good next step. Effective treatments exist, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and medication when appropriate. You don’t have to manage this on your own.

Industry observers note that physical symptoms are a common part of anxiety. Anxiety activates the body’s stress response, which causes real changes like a faster heart rate, muscle tension, and altered breathing. Many people with anxiety notice at least some physical symptoms alongside the mental ones. If they’re frequent or getting in the way of daily life, it’s worth talking with a doctor or mental health professional.

Sources indicate that “Anxiety attack” isn’t a clinical term, but people use it to describe anxiety that builds until it feels overwhelming, usually in response to a stressor like a looming deadline or a tense situation. The physical symptoms can include a rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, muscle tension, trembling, dry mouth, dizziness, and nausea. These sensations can be distressing, but they tend to ease as the stressful situation passes or your anxiety settles.

💙 If you’ve experienced the symptoms of an anxiety attack, here’s how to recover and take care of yourself.

Some anxiety symptoms feel strange because the stress response affects many parts of the body at once. For example, fast breathing can cause tingling in your hands. Or you might have a feeling of unreality or disconnection (called dissociation). Muscle tension might make it feel like your throat is closing. These varied symptoms can all have anxiety as the common cause. Of course, if they’re upcoming, intense, or don’t fit your usual anxiety symptoms, it’s best to check in with a doctor.

💙 Explore lesser-known symptoms of anxiety (some might surprise you!).

It has been revealed that when symptoms hit, the quickest relief usually comes through your breath. Make your out-breath longer than your in-breath—for example, breathing in for a count of four and out for six—and repeat for a minute or two. A longer exhale nudges your body out of the stress response and toward its rest-and-digest state.

Grounding works too. The 5–4–3–2–1 method has you name what you can see, touch, hear, smell, and taste, which pulls your focus out of anxious thoughts and back to the room around you.

Anxiety can affect the body as well as the mind, and for some people the physical side is what dominates, with few or no obvious worries attached. Your stress response can switch on faster than your conscious mind registers what set it off, so a racing heart or churning stomach can come before, or even without, any clear anxious thought.

It has been revealed that these physical symptoms are still part of anxiety, and the same tools, like slow breathing and grounding, can help calm them. If they’re newly introduced or unexplained, see a doctor to rule out other causes, such as thyroid problems, heart rhythm changes, or the effects of caffeine or medication.

It’s worth speaking with a doctor if your anxiety symptoms are newly introduced and unexplained, severe or getting worse, or affecting your day-to-day life. Some symptoms, like chest pain, shortness of breath, and heart palpitations, should be evaluated medically to rule out other causes, even if you suspect anxiety. A doctor can also refer you to a mental health professional if that would help.

If you’re experiencing sudden or severe chest pain, or chest pain with sweating, shortness of breath, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw, seek emergency care.

In a recent development, A worry loop is a cycle where anxiety feeds on itself. One anxious thought leads to another, and the more attention it gets, the stronger it grows.

According to recent reports, for example, an anxious thought sets off a physical sensation, that sensation becomes the focus of fresh worry (“Why is my heart racing? What’s wrong with me?”), and the worry drives more symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that breaking the loop usually means addressing both the mind and the body. You can calm the body directly with breathing and grounding, or use cognitive approaches like CBT to interrupt the thought patterns that keep the cycle going.

It has been revealed that mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • These foods contain both fibre and protein, which may help explain why they were linked to weight loss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These foods contain both fibre and protein, which may help explain why they were linked to weight loss.

These foods contain both fibre and protein, which may help explain why they were linked to weight loss.

Beans, lentils and chickpeas may help people lose weight and trim their waistlines, according to a review of 36 randomised trials.

Adults who ate diets containing these foods lost about a kilogram more than those on comparison diets.

Their waists also shrank by about 1.6 centimetres more on average.

One reason may be that beans and lentils deliver both fibre and protein, which can help a meal feel more filling.

If people feel satisfied after eating, they may find it easier to eat less later in the day.

The researchers brought together trials in which adults were randomly assigned to diets containing legumes other than soya or to a comparison diet.

The trials covered a range of pulses, including dried beans, peas, chickpeas and lentils.

That makes the findings relevant to several familiar foods, although the pooled result tells us little about how a serving of lentils stacks up against a serving of chickpeas.

The researchers looked at body weight, waist circumference, body fat and body mass index, which relates a person’s weight to their height.

The results pointed to modest reductions in weight and waist size, with a reduction in body fat in the trials that measured it.

A bowl of lentil soup and a bowl of soup made with refined grains can feel quite different to eat, partly because lentils bring fibre and protein to the meal.

The researchers suggest that these nutrients could help people feel satisfied and reduce how much they go on to eat.

What the beans or lentils replace may matter as well.

Replacing some of the rice in a meal with chickpeas gives you a different mix of foods from adding chickpeas to your usual portion of rice.

That distinction helps explain why the comparison diets matter when interpreting the results.

The study was published in the journal Food Science & Nutrition (Rahmanian et al., 2026).

#161974. The Art of Releasing Resentment in Your ADHD Relationship

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (927 w)
📖 Baca

The Art of Releasing Resentment in Your ADHD Relationship

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ADHD can complicate communication, expectations, and daily routines between partners.
  • Resentment – the anger, bitterness, and disappointment that build from the feeling we’ve been wronged and treated unfairly over time – is a slowly simmering emotion.
  • In a recent development, in relationships touched by ADHD, traits like forgetfulness, disorganization, and inconsistent follow-through can hasten these feelings and chip away at intimacy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ADHD can complicate communication, expectations, and daily routines between partners. Here’s how to spot resentment and take steps toward healing and reconnection.

Resentment – the anger, bitterness, and disappointment that build from the feeling we’ve been wronged and treated unfairly over time – is a slowly simmering emotion. Eventually, its toxic burn clouds the way we view our relationship and may even suffocate it.

In a recent development, in relationships touched by ADHD, traits like forgetfulness, disorganization, and inconsistent follow-through can hasten these feelings and chip away at intimacy. ADHD partners, in turn, commonly resent their neurotypical partners for misunderstanding the condition and setting unrealistic expectations.

Resentment is a protective, multilayered emotion that deserves reflection. Follow these steps to gradually untangle the complex feelings you may be harboring about your partner so you can let go of resentment and start healing.

Resentment is a defense mechanism. Landing a sarcastic comment, giving the silent treatment, or thinking, “Because you didn’t do X, I won’t do Y,” helps us feel in control. These behaviors allow us to avoid confronting difficult feelings and situations, though they eventually backfire and sow deeper resentment. Become clear-eyed about resentment’s function in your relationship so you can opt for more productive responses instead.

[Get This Free Download: Manage ADHD’s Impact on Your Relationship].

It has been revealed that do you resent your partner for any specific behaviors (or lack thereof)? Peel back the layers on this. Resentment often sits on top of hurt, fear, shame, helplessness, and other uncomfortable feelings. It means that something crucial to you feels threatened, ignored, or unmet.

For each pain point, think about what lies underneath. What do your partner’s actions trigger in you? What stories are you telling yourself about their behavior? Some examples include:.

“They leave all the planning to me.”.

“I feel like a child in this relationship.”.

“I feel more like a parent than a partner.”.

“My partner doesn’t respect how I do things or who I am.”.

“I resent feeling like the family project.”.

“My partner did something long ago and hasn’t apologized adequately.”.

[Read: 9 Ways ADHD May Strain Relationships].

Resolving resentment won’t happen overnight. Acceptance and forgiveness are distinct processes that can help dissolve resentment, but they work differently. If forgiveness feels too “massive,” go for the route of acceptance. If one partner keeps forgetting things, for example, asking for forgiveness every time can feel exhausting for both people. Acceptance notes: “This is a feature of our relationship that I need to plan around” rather than “I need to forgive you 50 times.”.

Miscommunication in neurodiverse relationships often comes from assumptions we make about our partners. We assume they process the world as we do and can read our minds. Review the following steps with your partner to engage in a brief and insightful “learning conversation” about resentments:.

Speaker: When you seem to be upset and I ask you how you’re doing, you often say you’re feeling “fine.” That makes me feel anxious because I’m not sure it’s true.

Listener: So you feel anxious when I say I’m fine when you don’t perceive that to be the case… because you think I’m lying to you?

It has been revealed that speaker: You’re right that I do feel anxious, but I don’t worry so much that you’re lying to me. What I’m concerned about is that you’re not sharing your true self with me.

Listener: You feel that when I say “I’m fine,” I’m choosing not to open up to you… which makes you feel like I’m not comfortable with you and not invested in our relationship?

Speaker: Yes, that’s exactly it.

It has been revealed that what are you willing to relinquish? To decide, get clear about your boundaries. Terri Cole, LCSW, a psychotherapist who specializes in boundaries, asks us to define our values by the following:.

Things that matter to you but are highly flexible and negotiable. Rule of thumb: You’d be okay if you didn’t have them.

Recent findings suggest that our most vital wishes and goals. They relate to how we envision our life. Compromising on deep desires often leads to resentment.

According to recent reports, behaviors, values, or situations that are fundamentally unacceptable to you. Crossing them usually means the relationship ends.

Sources indicate that there are no right or wrong answers. A dealbreaker to one person may be a preference to another.

Consider where your resentments about your partner fit within your system. If you decide that something is a non-concern, create boundaries – rules that you set for yourself, not your partner.

Example: You’ve decided to let go of resentment about your partner’s untidiness. Your boundary: “What’s on their side of the room is their responsibility to clean.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that when winter hits, it’s no surprise that many of us ditch our workout routines and reach for the hot cocoa instead.
  • In a recent development, staying active during the colder months doesn’t have to mean pushing yourself to the max or braving harsh conditions if that’s not your thing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Ah winter. It’s dark out, cold, and there’s a biting wind whistling down the street. Wanna grab your running shoes and start pounding the pavement? We didn’t think so.

It has been revealed that when winter hits, it’s no surprise that many of us ditch our workout routines and reach for the hot cocoa instead. And while it’s normal to feel a little unmotivated as the weather shifts, winter exercise doesn’t just help us stay fit, it can help us manage stress and keep our energy levels up. Exercising during the winter can also boost your mood — which can be super important if the cold temps and long nights get you down.

In a recent development, staying active during the colder months doesn’t have to mean pushing yourself to the max or braving harsh conditions if that’s not your thing. There are plenty of ways to make winter workouts more fun and enjoyable. With a few small adjustments, you could soon start to notice how much better you feel during this time of year.

Winter can feel tough on our bodies and minds, with shorter days, less sunlight, and colder temperatures. These changes can make us feel more tired, sluggish, or even a little down. This is especially true if you get the “winter blues” or seasonal affective disorder (SAD), where the lack of sunlight means your mood and energy levels take a dive. (At the moment in a funk? These nine tips can help shift a low mood.).

Exercise can play a massive role in managing these wintertime challenges because moving your body can trigger the release of natural mood-boosting chemicals, fight stress and help you to think more clearly.

Sources indicate that getting active in the winter can also improve sleep and help regulate your sleep-wake cycle, so even if you’re feeling thrown off by the longer nights and early darkness, exercise can help you get the rest you need to start your mornings on the right foot. Cue a good mood and steady energy throughout the day too!

Finding the right workouts for winter doesn’t mean you have to head out into the cold — but you can if you want to!

In a recent development, there are so many options you can enjoy indoors—even on the chilliest days—depending on what feels best for you. These are ten great winter workouts that’ll keep your body moving, boost your energy, and help you feel your best.

Sources indicate that ideal for warming up stiff muscles and relieving stress, plus, you don’t need much space or equipment — just a mat or a soft carpet. Check out online classes and videos for beginner to expert workouts.

According to recent reports, use dumbbells, resistance bands, or your body weight — or grab a can of tomatoes from your cupboard! Try exercises like lunges, squats, and push-ups indoors, so you can maintain or build muscle without braving the cold.

Recent findings suggest that if you have access to equipment, enjoy cardio without the cold. These machines let you set a steady pace, so you can up your fitness without overdoing things.

According to recent reports, dancing is great fun, but it’s also a fantastic cardio workout. Try a virtual dance class or follow a YouTube tutorial for a quick, energetic session to get your heart pumping and your face smiling. You can even invite your friends over for an 80s aerobic dance party and dress the part too!

It has been revealed that 💙 Only have five minutes? Add Mel Mah’s Dance Break to your routine.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re up for some fresh air, bundle up and head out for a winter hike. It’s a great way to explore nature, and the cold will likely feel refreshing once you start moving. Just be sure to dress in layers and check the weather before heading out.

Ice skating might look effortless, but it’s a solid workout for your legs and core. Many local rinks are open during the winter, and even if you’re a beginner, it can help you stay active and try something fresh. Make it social and see if your coworkers want to join you for a weekly session after work to help keep you motivated.

With the right winter gear, running outside can be invigorating. Layer up in moisture-wicking clothes to keep comfortable, and watch for icy spots to stay safe.

💙 Try Mel Mah’s Mindful Run to experience 20 minutes of running with intention.

According to recent reports, if you have snow where you live, give cross-country skiing a try. It’s a full-body workout that’s low impact, making it gentle on the joints and awesome for the eyes. It’s the perfect way to soak in the beautiful scenery and the fresh air of a winter wonderland.

Pilates strengthens core muscles and improves flexibility, and like yoga, it doesn’t need much space or equipment. Follow an online session to get a workout that supports your whole body, or practice some basic moves on your own.

In a recent development, combine bursts of high-intensity exercise with rest intervals to get a lot of action in a short space of time. These workouts can be easy to do at home and don’t require any equipment, just a little space for a few dynamic moves.

Industry observers note that once you've picked a few workouts, the next hurdle is getting yourself to do them. We get it. These six tips may help you stay motivated and safe while you exercise in colder weather.

Recent findings suggest that start by setting small, achievable goals that feel right for the season. Winter can be more about maintaining your fitness and feeling good rather than pushing for significant gains or intense goals.

Decide on manageable goals like working out three times a week or moving for 20 minutes a day so they feel achievable, and don’t forget to leave room for flexibility.

And when you’re really struggling, aim to just get started. Once you’ve got your sneakers on, you might find it easier to begin that workout. Be gentle with yourself and listen to what feels best for your body and mind — some days might feel easier than others, and that’s completely normal. These seven tips can help you push through a workout mentally.

Industry observers note that decide on a time that suits your energy levels and lifestyle—like in the morning, during lunch, or in the evening—and stay consistent. When you make exercise a regular part of your day, you’re less likely to have to force yourself to do it.

And remember, it’s okay if some days don’t go as planned — just get back to your routine the next day.

If you plan to workout outside, layer up your clothing to stay comfortable and dry as it can make winter exercise much more enjoyable.

Start with a breathable, moisture-wicking base layer, add a mid-layer for insulation, and finish with a wind-proof, waterproof outer for protection from the elements. Add gloves, a hat, and warm socks to keep your fingers and toes cozy and safe, too.

Even if you’re just heading out to a studio down the street, make sure to dress warmly so that once you’re done sweating, you don’t catch a cold.

Cold weather makes muscles tighter, which can increase your risk of injury. To help prevent this, start every workout with a warm-up, especially if you’re outside. Spend 5–10 minutes doing dynamic stretches or gentle movements like walking in place, jumping jacks, or arm circles to get your blood flowing and prepare your muscles.

A good warm-up loosens up your body, reduces stiffness, and gets you ready for the main part of your workout.

Sources indicate that when you venture out for your exercise, see if a friend wants to join you so you can catch up while you work out or grab a coffee after a class. The shared experience can boost your mood and keep you going, even on days when it’s tough to get moving.

It has been revealed that no real-life takers? Look for online fitness classes, join a virtual exercise challenge, or check if a friend wants to work out “together” by video call. Virtual communities can create accountability, which can help you stick to your goals. And who knows, you might even make a new friend out of it, too!

Staying active in winter deserves a celebration! Treat yourself when you hit small milestones — have a seasonal-spiced herbal tea after a workout, click “buy” on that latest piece of workout gear you’ve been eyeing for months now, or become your own DJ and make a fun, feel-good playlist to exercise to.

Rewards can make the experience more enjoyable and give you something to look forward to. Even simple treats, like watching an episode of a favorite show or getting into comfy clothes post-workout, can help you recognize your efforts and build positive vibes around your winter workouts.

It can be tempting to start your outdoor exercise at a sprint because it’s so cold out, but that might risk stiffness and injury in cold muscles.

You’ll need to warm up first, so begin with 5–10 minutes of dynamic movements to gradually increase your heart rate and warm up your muscles.

If stepping out in sub-freezing temperatures to do your gentle movements doesn’t sound appealing (and we don’t blame you,) warm up inside before you head outdoors.

During colder months, there are lots of ways you can stay in shape and boost your mood by getting active:.

Stay warm by working out indoors.

Whether you venture down the block to the gym or stay at home, these indoor exercises need minimal space and equipment.

Brave the cold and get outdoors.

Sources indicate that it might be chilly, but there’s still joy and beauty in the winter — and exercise options available whether you’re close to nature or city-based. Make sure you’ve got proper gear and choose safe paths.

To prevent winter injuries, a few simple but notable steps can help you take care of yourself.

Dress warmly in layered, moisture-wicking clothes to keep muscles warm and flexible. Make sure you warm up with gentle cardio or dynamic stretching to get blood flowing, as cold muscles are prone to strain.

When outdoors, avoid icy or uneven surfaces and use footwear with a good grip for stability. Most importantly, listen to your body — if something feels off, don't push through it. Instead, adapt to your needs and take it day by day.

In a recent development, strangely, we tend to feel less thirsty in winter, even when we’re losing water during exercise. So stay aware and follow these easy tips to maintain hydration and support your body's performance and recovery.

Keep a water bottle handy and take small sips throughout your workout. You might even set reminders to drink water before, during, and after exercise. Also, if cold water is unappealing, opt for warm drinks like herbal tea or water with lemon to stay hydrated and warm.

If you’re feeling low because of the dark days and winter weather, you can combat winter blues with exercise, even if it’s just a little bit of movement. That’s because getting active can boost your mood and energy by releasing natural feel-good chemicals.

Set yourself a routine to get out for a walk in the fresh air (and sunshine, when the sun highlights its face) and gather your friends or family to make it a fun, social occasion, too — which can also help you stay accountable.

It has been revealed that prefer to stay indoors? Counteract shorter days by sitting near a window or using light therapy to lift your mood, and join a virtual fitness class for encouragement and connection. Be kind to yourself — every bit of self-care can help make winter brighter and healthier. (Take a look at these 20 self-care practices for inspo).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that so many of us live with jam-packed daily schedules, constantly juggling our responsibilities to work, family, and friends.
  • World Meditation Day, a day dedicated to uplifting the power of meditation and promoting regular acts of self-care, is the perfect opportunity to shift your focus back onto your mental well-being by prioritizing meditation and connecting with yourself through the hustle and bustle of everyday life.
  • According to recent reports, world Meditation Day is held each year on December 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.

Sources indicate that so many of us live with jam-packed daily schedules, constantly juggling our responsibilities to work, family, and friends. The never-ending to-do lists can wear us down, and any remaining free time we may have is spent zoning out in front of the TV or scrolling on our phones. Taking time to pause, breathe, and connect with ourselves may feel impossible, so sometimes we need an extra push.

World Meditation Day, a day dedicated to uplifting the power of meditation and promoting regular acts of self-care, is the perfect opportunity to shift your focus back onto your mental well-being by prioritizing meditation and connecting with yourself through the hustle and bustle of everyday life.

According to recent reports, world Meditation Day is held each year on December 21. It’s dedicated to the practice of meditation, a technique that’s been used for centuries to nurture a sense of calm and inner peace. The day is designed to promote awareness about the benefits of meditation and encourage people to bring the practice into their daily lives to restore a sense of balance and clarity.

Originating in India around 1500 B.C., meditation initially combined spirituality with the religious and philosophical life of Hindu and Buddhist traditions. The aim was to cultivate mindfulness and a deep, inward connection to the divine — or the inner self.

Meditation practices spread across Asia and to the Western world, where techniques were adapted to make them relevant to the unique spiritual, therapeutic, and practical needs of each culture.

Sources indicate that during World Meditation Day on December 21, people around the world acknowledge and celebrate the rich history and evolution of meditation. The day reminds us of meditation's ancient roots and its wide-ranging health and well-being benefits.

In December 2024, meditation got its own spot on the global calendar when the United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution proclaiming December 21 as World Meditation Day. The resolution invites people everywhere to observe the day in a way that suits them and to help raise awareness of the benefits of meditation.

Despite a long history, meditation is becoming more and more crucial in the modern world.

Stress reduction: Regular meditation may help decrease our level of stress hormones, like cortisol, helping to reduce stress and leading to improved mental health and decreased risk of stress-related diseases.

Enhanced concentration: Meditation can help train the brain to focus for longer periods, which can enhance productivity at work. This improved attention span can be extremely beneficial when we’re constantly bombarded with distractions and information.

Promotion of overall well-being: Meditation has been linked with many physical health benefits, including lowered blood pressure, reduced anxiety, and better immune system response.

Recent findings suggest that contribution to global harmony: By cultivating personal peace and mindfulness, meditation can encourage positive interactions. In this way, World Meditation Day helps promote unity across different cultures and communities.

Whether you’re an experienced meditator or newly introduced to the practice, taking part in World Meditation Day can be a fulfilling, enriching experience.

Many organizations host global meditation sessions on World Meditation Day. Connect with thousands of others around the world who are practicing meditation. This can be a powerful experience, emphasizing the unity and collective energy of the human experience.

Seek out workshops, either in-person or online, which can expose you to different meditation techniques and enhance your personal practice.

According to recent reports, initiative or attend a group meditation session at a local park, community center, or virtually. Group meditations can help build a sense of community and shared purpose, making the practice more enjoyable and impactful.

In a recent development, if you prefer solitude, dedicate specific time on World Meditation Day for your personal meditation practice. Create a special session where you focus on your intentions, gratitude, or personal peace, allowing you to connect with yourself on a deeper level.

It has been revealed that it’s always nice to share the positives in life, so why not spread the love by sharing your meditation experience on social media? Use the hashtag #WorldMeditationDay to join the trend. This can help spread awareness about the day and encourage others to get involved.

Here are a few ways you can enhance and deepen your own meditation practice in honor of World Meditation Day.

According to recent reports, if you’re fresh to meditation or prefer a structured approach, guided meditations can be helpful. An experienced practitioner directs you through spoken instructions, often accompanied by calming music or natural sounds. Try a guided meditation to help you focus, explore different techniques, or maintain meditation discipline.

💙 Add the Daily Calm to your meditation routine, for a newly introduced 10-minute guided meditation each day.

According to recent reports, establishing a specific area in your home for meditation can significantly improve the quality of your practice and be a reminder to pause and reconnect with yourself. Make your space quiet, comfortable, and free from distractions. You can even personalize it with items that promote relaxation and peace such as cushions, candles, incense, or soothing artwork.

Sources indicate that explore different styles of meditation to help keep your practice fresh and engaging. Beyond the commonly known mindfulness and transcendental meditation, you might try types like zen, vipassana, or heart-centered meditation, which offer their own benefits.

💙 Dive into Practices: Meditation for Beginners, a 7-day guided meditation series, to expand your practice.

Recent findings suggest that meditation doesn't always have to be a separate part of your day. Add mindfulness techniques into daily activities like walking, eating, or even during breaks at work to help you stay present throughout the day.

💙 Explore how meditation can be practiced during your 9-5 with the Mindfulness at Work series.

Recent findings suggest that engaging with fellow meditators can provide support, motivation, and deeper insight into your practice. Look for online forums and local groups that offer meetings, discussions, and shared meditation sessions, which can be particularly enriching.

💙 Join the Daily Calm Community on Facebook to engage with other meditators and share questions and experiences from your practice.

It has been revealed that while meditation has been around for centuries, the origin of World Meditation Day isn’t clear. World Meditation Day has been observed for many years and has grown in popularity across the globe in recent years as more people have embraced the practices and recognized their benefits.

We celebrate World Meditation Day to recognize and promote the many benefits of meditation. These benefits can include reducing stress, improving concentration, enhancing emotional health, and building a sense of peace and community. The day encourages new and seasoned meditators to dedicate time to their meditation practices and to positively impact personal and global well-being.

If you’re organizing a meditation event in your community, a few simple steps can help make your event a success.

Start by choosing a suitable location such as a community center, park, or an online platform.

Next, decide on the format of the event — for example, a guided meditation, silent meditation, or a workshop with a knowledgeable instructor.

Promote the event through local community boards, social media, and word of mouth.

Provide clear instructions about what participants should bring (such as mats or cushions) and what they should expect from the event.

These resources can make it easy to bring meditation into your daily routine, no matter where in the world you are or how experienced you are.

Do you work from home? Here's how to stay focused (and sane)

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1477 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, your commute is a 10-step walk from your bedroom to your desk.
  • According to recent reports, but working from home can also bring up challenges that add up over time, such as a lack of boundaries between work and rest and days that feel lonely.
  • Ahead, we’ll cover how to stay focused and connected while working from home, whether you went remote last month or years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

In a recent development, your commute is a 10-step walk from your bedroom to your desk. The coffee's freshly brewed, and you’re still in your pajama pants. For many people, these types of comforts are the benefit of working from home.

According to recent reports, but working from home can also bring up challenges that add up over time, such as a lack of boundaries between work and rest and days that feel lonely. Luckily, the habits you build around your workday can help ease both.

Ahead, we’ll cover how to stay focused and connected while working from home, whether you went remote last month or years ago.

According to recent reports, working from home has upsides and downsides, and you may notice both in the same week. On the plus side:.

Time and energy back: Without a commute, you may have more time and energy for the rest of your day.

Higher productivity: In a randomized study, employees who worked from home performed about 13% better than those in the office.

It has been revealed that flexibility without a career cost: In a follow-up study, employees who worked from home two days a week performed as well as their in-office coworkers and were promoted as often. They were also less likely to quit.

Risk of isolation: In a large 2026 study in Science, remote work was linked to about a third of the rise in isolation and mental distress.

Blurred boundaries: Without a commute or an office door, your workday can stretch into evenings and weekends.

Higher burnout rates: In a review of 44 studies from the pandemic years, remote workers often reported burnout.

Small changes to your setup can help you get into work mode. Whether you’re building your first home workspace or refreshing one you’ve used for years, these tweaks can make your workday feel smoother.

A dedicated spot: Pick one place to work, such as the corner of a room or one end of the table. Your brain may start to associate that spot with work.

It has been revealed that natural light: Set up near a window if you can. Morning daylight may help you feel alert during the day and sleep better at night. If you don’t have a window, a warm desk lamp paired with a bright overhead light may ease eye strain.

Physical comfort: Choose a supportive seat and raise your screen to eye level, so discomfort doesn’t pull your attention away. A cushion behind your lower back or a firm pillow under you can stand in for a special chair. If sitting for long stretches is hard on your body, switch positions throughout the day or ask your doctor about seating options that fit your needs.

Fewer distractions: Clear your work surface of anything you don’t need for the task at hand. Close extra browser tabs and silence phone notifications, since digital clutter may pull at your focus in the same way physical clutter does.

Sources indicate that sounds for focus: Some people work best in silence, while others prefer instrumental music or ambient sound in the background. In a noisy home, headphones or earplugs can muffle the commotion. If those don’t work for you, a closed door or a “focus time” sign can let the people you live with know you’re concentrating.

💙 Explore how lo-fi music can support your focus.

Working from home takes away some of the structure an office provides, but a solid routine can bring a bit of it back. Here are a few ideas worth trying:.

Air Pollution Reprograms Brain Immune Cells, Raises Dementia Risk by 25%

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A newly introduced study reveals that fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) raises dementia risk by 25% and triggers Alzheimer’s-like brain damage even without amyloid plaques.
  • In a recent development, microscopic soot, industrial emissions, and wildfire smoke, collectively categorized as fine particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), have long been recognized as major drivers of cardiovascular and respiratory disease.
  • Now, a comprehensive translational study published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation by researchers at Case Western Reserve University, University Hospitals, and the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center provides compelling human and experimental evidence that air pollution directly fuels neurodegeneration by hijacking the brain’s immune system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A newly introduced study reveals that fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) raises dementia risk by 25% and triggers Alzheimer’s-like brain damage even without amyloid plaques. The research shows that inhaled pollution reprograms the brain’s resident immune cells (microglia), compromises the blood-brain barrier, drains cellular energy reserves, and kills newborn neurons in the hippocampus.

Source: Case Western Reserve University.

In a recent development, microscopic soot, industrial emissions, and wildfire smoke, collectively categorized as fine particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), have long been recognized as major drivers of cardiovascular and respiratory disease. Mounting epidemiological evidence has also linked polluted air to cognitive decline, yet whether inhaled particles actively cause dementia, and precisely how they injure the brain, has remained an urgent scientific question.

Now, a comprehensive translational study published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation by researchers at Case Western Reserve University, University Hospitals, and the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center provides compelling human and experimental evidence that air pollution directly fuels neurodegeneration by hijacking the brain’s immune system.

It has been revealed that led by co-senior authors Dr. Sanjay Rajagopalan and Dr. Andrew Pieper, the research team combined population-scale human health tracking with controlled five-month inhalation experiments in mice to map the cellular chain reaction linking dirty air to dementia.

To quantify how long-term air pollution exposure shapes dementia risk across diverse genetic backgrounds, the researchers analyzed medical and environmental records from roughly 500,000 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank, tracked for up to 14 years.

Industry observers note that even after controlling for confounding variables, including age, smoking status, diabetes, and socioeconomic factors—people residing in the most polluted third of geographic regions were 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease or a related dementia than those living in the cleanest third. Crucially, high air pollution elevated dementia risk regardless of whether an individual carried high or low inherited genetic risk for Alzheimer’s.

To test causation directly, the investigators exposed mice to real-world outdoor Cleveland air for five months, concentrating PM2.5 particles to match levels recorded in the world’s most heavily polluted urban centers.

Even in otherwise healthy mice without genetic predispositions to neurodegeneration, chronic PM2.5 exposure triggered widespread brain pathology:.

Recent findings suggest that remarkably, these memory deficits and Alzheimer’s-like cellular injuries emerged in healthy mice completely devoid of amyloid plaques. When the researchers exposed mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer’s pathology to the same polluted air, the particles inflicted identical neuroinflammatory and metabolic damage while simultaneously accelerating amyloid plaque accumulation.

Sources indicate that “By recreating in mice what happens when people breathe polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain’s immune cells,” explained Rajagopalan, professor of medicine and director of the Cardiovascular Research Institute at Case Western Reserve School of Medicine. “These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world’s population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it.”.

In a recent development, “We’ve identified a key way that air pollution harms the healthy brain and speeds up Alzheimer’s disease,” added Pieper, director of the Harrington Discovery Institute Brain Health Medicines Center and psychiatrist at the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center. “This helps us understand how factors in our environment can accelerate and intensify brain diseases of aging. It also opens the door to studying other environmental stresses on the brain, and to finding ways to keep the brain resilient even when we can’t avoid those stressors.”.

How much does air pollution increase the risk of developing dementia?

In an analysis of nearly 500,000 adults tracked for up to 14 years, researchers found that people living in areas with the highest levels of fine particulate air pollution were 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease or related dementias than those in the cleanest areas, even among people with low genetic risk.

What does fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) physically do to the brain?

In mouse experiments recreating urban air pollution, inhaled PM2.5 particles caused the blood-brain barrier to leak, triggered brain inflammation, lowered cellular energy reserves (NAD+/NADH ratio), killed newborn memory neurons in the hippocampus, and reprogrammed the genes of the brain’s immune cells (microglia).

Does air pollution only harm brains that already have Alzheimer’s plaques?

Sources indicate that no. Researchers were struck to find that air pollution caused memory problems, immune cell disruption, and neuron death in healthy mice that had no amyloid plaques at all, while also speeding up plaque buildup in mice genetically prone to Alzheimer’s disease.

Air pollution exposure interacts with Alzheimer’s genetic susceptibility to reshape microglial epigenomic and transcriptional programs.

Chronic exposure to fine particulate matter air pollution (PM2.5) is associated with cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease, but the biology connecting inhaled particles to the brain remains incompletely defined. Among 475,325 eligible UK Biobank participants, long-term PM2.5 exposure and Alzheimer disease (AD) polygenic risk were both independently associated with higher risk of AD and related dementias (ADRD).

The PM2.5-by-polygenic risk score (PRS) interaction in Cox models was statistically significant but sub-multiplicative or below unity (interaction HR 0.981, 95% CI 0.965–0.998; p = 0.026), indicating that the combined association was smaller than the simple product of the two individual associations.

It has been revealed that to define the underlying biology, we exposed 5xFAD mice, an amyloid-based model of AD, and wild-type (WT) littermates to concentrated ambient PM2.5 or filtered air for 20 weeks. PM2.5 exposure activated microglia, disrupted the blood-brain barrier, depleted the brain NAD+/NADH pool required for resilience and repair, impaired postnatal hippocampal neurogenesis, and caused cognitive deficits.

In 5xFAD mice it additionally increased amyloid burden. Paired RNA-seq and ATAC-seq of microglia isolated from the same animals demonstrated that exposure remodeled both gene expression and chromatin accessibility, and that that magnitude and direction of this response depended on genotype, converging on inflammatory, lysosomal, oxidative-stress, synaptic, and amyloid-related pathways.​.

​These population-scale data in humans and experimental data in mice​ support PM2.5 as an environmental neurotoxicant and define microglial regulatory programs through which genetic background shapes the biological response to a common and modifiable exposure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swiss watchmaker Mondaine has expanded its Doppio collection with the Solar Skeleton, a timepiece that brings solar technology into the foreground of its design.

Rather than concealing the solar plates beneath the dial, the watch reveals them through a precisely cut circular opening, turning a functional component into a defining visual feature.

The design builds on the distinctive visual language of Mondaine‘s Doppio collection, which is characterised by double-line hands and indexes, a concave dial and a double-domed sapphire crystal.

Mondaine explained that these elements establish a sense of repetition, rhythm and structural clarity, while the exposed solar plates introduce an additional layer of depth and visual interest.

While solar technology is typically hidden from view, Mondaine has taken a different approach with the Doppio Solar Skeleton.

A carefully positioned circular opening around the centre of the dial offers a controlled view of the solar movement, while the outer section retains the indexes to ensure clear readability.

By making the technology visible, Mondaine aimed to bridge the watch’s technical function with its aesthetic identity, without compromising the “clarity and legibility” that define the collection.

Powered by a Swiss Ronda solar movement, the watch converts natural and artificial light into electrical energy, which is stored in a rechargeable battery.

According to Mondaine, a few minutes of sunlight can reactivate a fully discharged movement, while a full charge provides a power reserve of up to eight months in complete darkness.

The brand explained that this technology eliminates the need for regular battery replacements, offering a more resource-conscious approach to timekeeping.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton is available in two versions, each offering a different interpretation of its distinctive design.

The first combines a polished silver 316L stainless steel case with a vegan grape leather strap, bringing together traditional watchmaking materials and a contemporary material alternative.

The second features a polished black stainless steel case paired with a matching mesh bracelet, creating a more monochromatic appearance that emphasises the watch’s clean lines and geometric detailing.

Both versions feature a 41-millimetre case, a discreet date window and a precisely laser-etched Mondaine logo and solar markings.

A double-domed sapphire crystal and water resistance of up to 5 ATM complete the design, “combining refined aesthetics with everyday practicality”.

“With the Doppio Solar Skeleton, we wanted to make solar technology part of the design itself,” noted Mondaine.

“By revealing the cells beneath the dial, we have created a watch where functionality becomes a defining aesthetic feature, while staying true to Mondaine’s principles of clarity, precision and Swiss design.”.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton reflects Mondaine’s commitment to iconic Swiss minimalist design, where form and function work together.

By integrating visible solar technology into the collection’s established design language, the watch intends to demonstrate how a functional element can become an integral part of a timepiece’s aesthetic identity.

To find out more about Mondaine and the Doppio Solar Skeleton, visit the brand’s website.
