Why Nerve Pain Lingers

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that researchers uncovered a molecular pathway in the spinal cord that drives persistent neuropathic pain long after an initial nerve injury.
  • Source: Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine.
  • For millions of people living with neuropathic pain, even a feather-light touch or a mild shift in temperature can ignite excruciating discomfort long after an initial physical injury has healed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that researchers uncovered a molecular pathway in the spinal cord that drives persistent neuropathic pain long after an initial nerve injury. The multi-omics and electrophysiological study reveals that nerve injury suppresses the nuclear regulatory protein Nono, triggering a steep drop in Kcnq2 potassium channels that normally calm spinal pain neurons, while restoring Nono reverses pain hypersensitivity in animal models.

Source: Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine.

For millions of people living with neuropathic pain, even a feather-light touch or a mild shift in temperature can ignite excruciating discomfort long after an initial physical injury has healed. Rather than stemming solely from ongoing tissue damage at the original wound site, persistent nerve pain is frequently driven by central sensitization, a state in which pain-processing circuits inside the spinal cord become hyperexcitable and amplify ordinary sensory signals.

Now, a comprehensive study published in Research by scientists at Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Fudan University, and partner institutions has pinpointed a critical molecular switch behind this spinal hyperexcitability: the Nono–Kcnq2 regulatory axis.

By combining five layers of molecular profiling with single-neuron electrophysiology and behavioral testing, the team demonstrated how nerve injury silences a vital genetic brake inside spinal neurons—and indicated that restoring this pathway alleviates chronic pain sensitivity.

Under healthy conditions, neurons in the spinal cord’s dorsal horn rely on specialized potassium channels to stabilize their electrical charge and prevent runaway firing. When potassium ions flow out of a neuron, they keep excitability in check; when those channels disappear, neurons fire rapidly in response to minimal stimulation.

In a recent development, to trace why potassium channel control breaks down after nerve trauma, the investigators examined a rat model of chronic sciatic nerve constriction, which produces pronounced mechanical and thermal pain sensitivity within three days. Electrophysiological recordings confirmed that spinal dorsal horn neurons fired far more readily while exhibiting sharply diminished outward potassium currents.

Applying an integrated multi-omics pipeline, spanning proteomics, phosphoproteomics, transcription factor profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and single-cell RNA sequencing across 48,279 spinal cord cells, the researchers mapped the exact cellular shifts occurring at seven and 21 days post-injury:.

Industry observers note that molecular binding experiments confirmed that Nono directly binds to a conserved region of the Kcnq2 gene promoter to drive its expression. To test whether repairing this broken link could relieve pain, the researchers delivered an adenoviral vector carrying Nono into the spinal region of nerve-injured rats.

Increasing Nono expression successfully rebuilt Kcnq2 protein abundance, restored protective outward potassium currents in dorsal horn neurons, and significantly eased mechanical and thermal pain hypersensitivity. When the team applied XE991, a selective pharmacological blocker of Kcnq2/3 potassium channels, both the restored potassium currents and the behavioral pain relief were largely reversed, confirming that Nono alleviates pain specifically by reactivating Kcnq2 channels.

While the researchers emphasize that clinical therapies remain a long-term goal—noting that experiments were conducted in male rats and that additional pathways also contribute to neuropathic pain—the findings illuminate a clear mechanistic bridge linking gene transcription to electrical excitability in the spinal cord.

Rather than merely masking pain signals with broad analgesics, future therapies aimed at preserving Nono activity or supporting Kcnq2 potassium channel function could help quiet overactive spinal circuits at their molecular source.

Why can neuropathic pain persist even after a nerve injury has healed?

Following nerve trauma, neurons in the spinal cord can undergo central sensitization, becoming abnormally excitable so that they amplify harmless signals like light touch or mild warmth into intense pain.

What did researchers discover about the Nono and Kcnq2 proteins in the spinal cord?

In a recent development, scientists found that nerve injury reduces the activity of the nuclear protein Nono, which normally switches on the Kcnq2 gene. Kcnq2 produces potassium channels that act like electrical brakes to calm spinal neurons; when Kcnq2 levels drop by up to 80%, pain neurons fire excessively.

Did restoring Nono reduce pain sensitivity in the animal study?

Yes. When researchers used a viral vector to restore Nono expression in the spinal cord of rats with nerve injuries, Kcnq2 potassium channel levels rebounded, neuronal firing calmed down, and the animals revealed significantly less sensitivity to mechanical and thermal pain.

Multi-Omics Analysis Reveals Nono–Kcnq2 Regulation of Neuronal Excitability in Chronic Constriction Injury-Induced Neuropathic Pain.

Neuropathic pain, resulting from somatosensory nervous system damage or disease, is a debilitating condition marked by spontaneous pain, hypersensitivity, and sensory abnormalities. Neuropathic pain involves spinal neuronal hyperexcitability, yet its molecular basis remains poorly defined.

We utilized a comprehensive multi-omics approach, incorporating proteomics, phosphoproteomics, concatenated tandem array of consensus transcription response elements, and both single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, to chart time-resolved adaptations in the L4 to L6 spinal cord of a chronic constriction injury rat model.

Multi-omics revealed remodeling of glutamatergic synapse pathways and identified non-POU (Pit-Oct-Unc) domain-containing octamer binding (Nono) as a down-regulated transcription factor associated with reduced potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily Q member 2 (Kcnq2) expression. Nono and Kcnq2 were co-enriched in neurexin 3-positive and peripherin-positive spinal neurons.

It has been revealed that restoring Nono expression up-regulated Kcnq2, enhanced K+ outward currents (an effect largely abolished by the Kcnq2/3 blocker XE991), and alleviated pain hypersensitivity. Mechanistically, Nono was enriched at a conserved Kcnq2 promoter region in vivo and enhanced Kcnq2 promoter activity in reporter assays.

Together, these findings established a Nono–Kcnq2 transcriptional axis that constrained spinal excitability and suggested a therapeutic entry point for neuropathic pain.

#161943. Breaking: Brain scans reveal which disorders are linked to faster brain aging

Breaking: Brain scans reveal which disorders are linked to faster brain aging

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People with dementia, mild cognitive impairment, alcohol addiction, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia may show signs of accelerated brain aging, according to a study published in the open access journal PLOS Medicine.
  • Researchers can estimate whether a person's brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age.
  • To investigate how different brain conditions might influence this measure, the researchers analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 45,900 controls drawn from several brain imaging databases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People with dementia, mild cognitive impairment, alcohol addiction, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia may show signs of accelerated brain aging, according to a study published in the open access journal PLOS Medicine. The research, led by Shile Qi of the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, China, found that different conditions appear to be associated with distinct patterns of aging across the brain.

Researchers can estimate whether a person's brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age. One way to do this is with predictive age difference (PAD), which compares a person's actual age with an age estimated from brain imaging. A positive PAD means the brain appears older than would typically be expected.

To investigate how different brain conditions might influence this measure, the researchers analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 45,900 controls drawn from several brain imaging databases. They compared those scans with data from 2,698 people with a range of conditions and differences, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), alcohol or tobacco addiction, Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or major depressive disorder.

Alzheimer's and MCI Show the Strongest Associations.

Among the conditions examined, the neurodegenerative disorders AD and MCI showed the strongest associations with higher PAD values, suggesting the greatest degree of accelerated brain aging.

Addiction and psychiatric disorders were also associated with increased PAD. By contrast, the researchers found no overall differences in PAD between controls and people with ADHD or ASD.

Different Disorders Affect Different Brain Regions.

The team also examined PAD across individual brain regions and looked at patterns of gene expression associated with the different conditions.

One area that stood out was the prefrontal cortex, which showed higher PAD across multiple brain disorders. Psychiatric disorders were associated with elevated PAD in the frontal and temporal lobes, while dementia was linked to higher PAD in the frontal and occipital cortex.

In a recent development, addiction highlighted a different pattern. Higher PAD was observed in the default mode network, as well as in the salience network, putamen and thalamus.

The researchers also identified differences in gene transcription associated with particular conditions and divergences, suggesting that the patterns of brain aging may be linked to distinct underlying biological processes.

A Potential Source of Future Biomarkers.

Recent findings suggest that the findings do not show that these conditions directly cause accelerated brain aging. The study is correlational, and some conditions, particularly psychiatric disorders and addiction, frequently occur together, which can make their individual effects difficult to separate.

Even so, the researchers suggest that studying PAD more closely could eventually help identify biomarkers associated with common brain disorders and provide upcoming clues about the biological pathways involved.

The authors add, "Different neurological disorders appear to leave different signatures on the brain aging clock, which may help researchers better understand the neural and biological pathways involved in these conditions.".

This work was supported by the Key Research and Development Strategy of Jiangsu Province, China (BE2023668) to S.Q., and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (62376124) to S.Q. The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that though Djurdja Padejski was raised in communist Yugoslavia, her life there felt stable and uneventful for a long time. In the 1980s, under Yugoslavia’s “soft” one-party government, Padejski and her friends read Western literature, watched Hollywood movies, and listened to the BBC.

“We grew up in a very comfortable, naive environment,” Padejski says.

Sources indicate that that changed in the 1990s when Yugoslavia split into several republics. Civil war broke out, and a virulent strain of nationalism took hold in Serbia, the Yugoslavian state where Padejski lived. Firebrand leader Slobodan Milošević ascended to power and began meddling in elections, targeting opposition leaders, and igniting ethnic cleansing campaigns.

“He captured the entire society and his party,” Padejski remembers. “Very soon I found myself on the streets protesting.” Padejski’s activism against repressive Serbian regimes would continue until 2011, when she and her husband, investigative journalist Djordje Padejski, left the country after people threatened to kill them.

Industry observers note that the Padejskis arrived in the U.S. with hard-won knowledge of how to outlast repression over the long haul. In recent years, they’ve tapped back into that knowledge and shared it with those around them as they witness here in America the illegal destruction of government agencies, election tampering, and warrantless arrests of citizens and non-citizens. This isn’t just true in the United States—around the world, democracy is declining.

Recent findings suggest that how can we go on defying rising authoritarianism when no clear endpoint is in sight? Psychology and motivation research complement the experience of people like the Padejskis by addressing how to conserve energy and sustain commitment to your ideals in challenging conditions.

“The goal of the authoritarian regime is to desensitize us to extremes, to things we should never agree with or consider normal,” says Djurdja Padejski, now a language and culture researcher (and doctoral candidate) at Arizona State University.

In a recent development, surviving repression depends on rejecting this presumed “normality” and refusing to let your inner state mirror extremes imposed from above. To that end, here are seven research-backed ways to subsist under indefinite duress.

Sources indicate that life under repression feels exhausting due to the colossal scale of so much of what is happening: attacks on the free press, denial of life-saving aid to millions overseas, ongoing ICE killings on the streets and in detention facilities. Reading about such developments understandably triggers feelings of overwhelm. Research finds that these feelings can drive people to shut down their emotions, dampening their motivation to help in concrete ways.

It has been revealed that djurdja Padejski has come to recognize that to avoid that trap, she has to face her human limits squarely without drowning in self-recrimination. As a young adult under Milošević’s rule, she learned early that worrying about what she couldn’t do was a waste of time and energy.

“It is very notable not to get stuck in that moment, not to be clutching your pearls,” she notes. “We have to be strategic to preserve our resources.”.

Industry observers note that admitting your own lack of control over the major picture can be a necessary prelude to taking the actions still available to you, Padejski claims. “We have to see [the situation] for what it is, so we can focus our efforts on keeping our minds, our bodies, and our communities as healthy as possible under the circumstances.”.

It has been revealed that once you’ve gotten clear about what is within your power to control, you can get granular by carrying out regular acts of “micro-resistance.” These acts of defiance do not require you to upend your daily rhythms or put your life on the line. They can be as simple as attending a march, supporting a neighbor at an immigration court visit, or wearing a shirt with a resistance slogan.

Micro-resistance acts—such as creating protest art and continuing to study even when their department was banned from the university—helped sustain both Padejskis through years of repression, reminding them of the power they had despite limits imposed from on high.

Recent findings suggest that “These micro-level actions add up,” Djordje Padejski writes. “Even small acts of defiance can maintain your sense of agency.”.

It has been revealed that self-described “small-time” lawyer Daniel Suitor excels at this kind of micro-resistance. During ICE raids in his hometown of Minneapolis, he channeled his overwhelm by signing up for a course on how to file legal paperwork to free unjustly detained Twin Cities residents.

In a recent development, after Suitor filed his first case, he found out surprisingly quickly that he’d won and that the man he was representing would be freed. That proof-of-concept case spurred him to file another legal petition, then several more in quick succession. And he wasn’t alone in his commitment: To date, Minnesota lawyers have filed more than 1,000 cases challenging unjust detentions.

Acts of micro-resistance can also help prime us for future courageous action. When people perform smaller acts of selflessness and service, large-scale heroism becomes easier to contemplate, explains Medical College of Wisconsin heroism researcher Zeno Franco. Concrete practice can make you more adept at translating abstract ideals into action.

Industry observers note that “You need to understand beyond theory,” Djurdja Padejski indicates. “We actually, as humans, can’t imagine how concepts work in [the] real world unless we experience them hands-on.”.

For the Padejskis, one of the most stifling aspects of life under Serbian autocracy was not knowing when the repression would lift, if at all.

Periods of confinement, literal or figurative, are more bearable when a clear endpoint is in sight, and indefinite periods of repression feel uniquely oppressive. A third or more of incarcerated people with open-ended sentences suffer from depression. Others feel rooted to the present moment, severed from any potential future.

It has been revealed that “I simply try to live in the here and now and not to initiative,” one prisoner told the University of Bern researcher Irene Marti, who studies open-ended confinement. “Because I don’t have any future or only one that is very far away.”.

When the endpoint of repression is uncertain, or when a challenging situation has no clear natural limit, creating your own intermediate endpoints can help you stay committed to your goals and values.

In a recent goal-setting study, when people broke an annual community service goal into granular sub-goals (say, four hours of service a week, or eight every two weeks), they volunteered more hours in the long run than people without intermediate goals.

In the same way, committed resisters can pledge to put in a set number of hours each week, or carry out a set number of clearly defined actions. According to self-determination theory, choosing and pursuing your own accessible goals boosts your well-being and motivation—internal changes that persist even when the larger crisis remains ongoing.

As governments around the world curtail freedom of speech and movement, it’s hard not to feel the noose tightening. One way to create more existential breathing room is to consider how this moment fits into the longer arc of history.

Industry observers note that this helps you subsist in the present by reminding you of parallel past moments (whether decades or centuries ago), how they came to a head, and what ultimately resolved them. Research finds that when people take a long-term perspective, reflecting on recent stressful events as though they happened far in the past, they report less emotional distress in the moment.

Sources indicate that djurdja Padejski found solace in doing this during Milošević’s reign. “I survived that period mostly by reading the columns in the newspapers,” she notes. One column in particular, by Serbian anthropologist Ivan Čolović, examined the regime’s activities from a broader historical and social perspective.

Recent findings suggest that “He was offering a vocabulary and a theoretical apparatus to help us deal with the horrors of civil war. The news about it was the most severely censored, the propaganda was relentless, and all of it was newly introduced for many of us who were children when the fallout of our world began,” Padejski says. “That’s how I survived with my sanity intact, because it helped me to recognize what is happening to society.”.

Among the most potent present-day energy drains is the social media industrial complex that feeds on people’s rage and frustration, serving up extreme viewpoints that deepen entrenched social divides as they rack up likes and views.

“Social media and internet platforms—they’re amplifying what is also a typical quality of authoritarian regimes. They’re all about grandiosity,” indicates Djurdja Padejski, who studies the linguistic mechanisms of propaganda. “Algorithms grab people’s attention by intensifying the language and the visuals and the overall framing.” That’s a massive reason why frequent social media use saps your cognitive resources and motivation, making it harder to subsist under repression.

Plugging this energy drain requires not just limiting your time online, but redirecting more of that time to the in-person, small-group exchange to which humans are uniquely suited.

In a recent development, when you engage with people face to face, it’s much harder to reduce them to a stereotype or particular viewpoint. And by getting to know them in all their messiness, contradiction, and complexity, you bond with them in ways that lighten the mental and practical load for everyone involved.

Recent findings suggest that “To resist this reduction of our existence to, ‘What are you for or against?’ means embracing creativity, art, friends, communal projects, protests, walks,” Padejski says. “These 10 years of resistance [in Serbia]—I honestly remember it as a series of walks. Sometimes that meant running away together from Milošević‘s militias or the official police, or from water cannons, or rubber bullets. But what is left is our conversations on ideas, on creations.”.

Though exchanges like these may not further resistance directly, they form the edifice that sustains it. Within bonded human-scale communities, members have a clear sense of not just their own energetic capacity, but that of others in the group. That means they can pinch-hit for one another: When someone needs help, they can fill in on the spot—or, like relay racers, take up the baton when someone needs to withdraw. This shared flexibility and responsiveness help all group members to stay committed for the long haul.

For the Padejskis, subsisting under Serbian repression meant homing in on the values that were most crucial to them, and upholding those values even if it meant sacrificing convenience or comfort. When Djordje Padejski needed a lifesaving drug, a relative told him he could work his connections to obtain the medicine, but only if Padejski joined the Serbian dictator’s political party. Padejski refused, knowing that doing so put his health at risk.

In a recent development, the couple have continued that tradition in the U.S., though in somewhat less life-altering ways. After Elon Musk unleashed an apparent Nazi salute at a Trump post-inauguration event, the Padejskis gave up their Tesla. “I drive a Subaru now,” Djurdja Padejski indicates. “I really don’t like it compared to Tesla, but I don’t regret it.”.

Some people write off such moral stands as more symbolic than substantive. But symbol, it turns out, shapes substance: What you stand for predicts and influences what you’ll do down the road, for good or ill. When people have a clear, consistent moral identity, studies find, they’re more likely to take real-world action aligned with that identity.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, when you’re willing to cave on something that seems minor, like supporting a complicit business, “you are detached from your inner beliefs, from what you know is real and good and safe,” Djurdja Padejski says. “Once you’re there, you are ready to compromise a lot of values that you think you are really one with.”.

One unexpected thing the Padejskis learned, under Milošević and afterward, was the importance of not swinging into action every time a devastating piece of news hit. Overcommitment amounted to self-sabotage, sapping energy and resources they’d need later on.

Industry observers note that military commanders have long known the importance of “keeping their powder dry,” Zeno Franco points out, holding back so they can act at the moment of maximum impact. In the same way, the best long-distance runners often hang back throughout a course to conserve energy, then uncork a burst of speed in the race’s final minutes.

According to recent reports, djurdja Padejski followed this principle to great effect under Milošević. She bided her time leading up to the critical elections of 2000, then worked tirelessly as an election volunteer to monitor for irregularities and make sure no one was falsifying results. All the while, ruling party members with guns lurked in the background.

According to recent reports, “This guy started opening his gun and checking the bullets, and we didn’t cave. We just ignored him,” Padejski says. “We knew we were risking our lives, but we really believed it’s now or never.” Serbia’s democratic opposition party ultimately won that election, causing Milošević’s downfall.

Padejski hopes democratic activists around the world will take a similar approach as crucial elections near. Under repressive conditions, keeping your powder dry “is not an instruction to put off action as long as possible, but rather the wisdom to know that being prepared to act at just the right moment may require careful guarding of resources and energy,” Franco claims. “Biding your time is not the same as surrender.”.

Elizabeth Svoboda is the author of What Makes a Hero?: The Surprising Science of Selflessness. Her upcoming book, The Art of Pacing, is about setting a sustainable pace in a speed-obsessed world.

Adolescent Brain Circuits Shape Lifelong Social Drive

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newly introduced research reveals that adolescence is a critical developmental window for a brain pathway linking the prefrontal cortex to the ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR).
  • Recent findings suggest that adolescence is widely recognized as a period of intense behavioral and social transformation, marked by heightened peer seeking, shifting relationships, and emotional turbulence.
  • Now, new findings from The Ohio State University Department of Psychology pinpoint a critical developmental window inside a pathway linking the brain’s executive command center to its reward hub: the prefrontal cortex–ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR) circuit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced research reveals that adolescence is a critical developmental window for a brain pathway linking the prefrontal cortex to the ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR). The study shows that temporarily quieting this reward-and-motivation circuit during adolescence leads to lasting social withdrawal in adulthood, shedding light on why psychiatric conditions like depression and schizophrenia often emerge during the teenage years.

Source: The Ohio State University.

Recent findings suggest that adolescence is widely recognized as a period of intense behavioral and social transformation, marked by heightened peer seeking, shifting relationships, and emotional turbulence. While neuroscientists have mapped early infant brain development in granular detail, the exact neural mechanisms sculpting social behavior during the teenage years remain far less understood.

Now, new findings from The Ohio State University Department of Psychology pinpoint a critical developmental window inside a pathway linking the brain’s executive command center to its reward hub: the prefrontal cortex–ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR) circuit.

Presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience, by lead author and doctoral candidate Katrina Lin alongside senior investigator Dr. Laurence Coutellier, the study demonstrates that disrupting PFC-vSTR maturation during adolescence permanently dampens adult social motivation.

To establish how social drive naturally evolves across the lifespan, Lin and Coutellier first measured spontaneous social investigation in both adolescent and adult mice, whose compressed three-week adolescent window enables researchers to trace developmental trajectories across adulthood.

According to recent reports, “I always say it’s like two dogs in a park. They start sniffing each other. They’re careful at first, and then they go into a different type of sniffing behavior,” explained Coutellier, associate professor of behavioral neuroscience at Ohio State. As predicted, adolescent mice exhibited substantially higher motivation to initiate social interaction than adult mice.

According to recent reports, “In humans it’s the same,” Coutellier noted. “A teenager loves to hang out with their friends, and they will seek this interaction. As adults, we will be more careful. We don’t approach a stranger just like that, and we’ll be more cautious about the way we interact. There’s still a strong social motivation, which is necessary for us to have social relationships, but there is less of it.”.

The prefrontal cortex, which governs decision-making, impulse control, and social reasoning, and does not finish maturing in humans until roughly age 25, sends direct signals to the ventral striatum, a core hub for reward processing and motivation.

To test whether adolescent maturation of this pathway is essential for adult sociability, the team selectively switched off activity in PFC-vSTR neurons in both male and female mice during either adolescence or adulthood:.

“We found that actually, yes, if we prevent the maturation of the frontal circuit to the striatum, when mice reach adulthood they have impaired social motivation,” Coutellier said.

It has been revealed that understanding how the PFC-vSTR pathway wires itself during adolescence carries significant implications for psychiatry. Conditions such as depression and schizophrenia frequently manifest during the teenage years, often preceded or accompanied by profound social withdrawal.

Next, Coutellier’s laboratory plans to examine how real-world environmental stressors, such as prolonged adolescent social isolation, alter the maturation of this circuit.

Industry observers note that “We can try to study what happens when our mice don’t get to socialize, and we can think about what happened during COVID-19, when teenagers were told to stay home and stop socializing to be safe. How did that impact this developmental trajectory of the social circuits?” Coutellier asked. “We’re trying to understand what genetic and environmental factors can make these symptoms arise at the time of adolescence — not before, and not in adulthood, but during that sensitive period of development.”.

What is the PFC-vSTR brain circuit, and what does it do?

In a recent development, the prefrontal cortex–ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR) circuit connects the prefrontal cortex (the brain’s decision-making and social control center) to the ventral striatum (a key hub for reward and motivation). During adolescence, this pathway matures to support healthy social motivation and peer interaction.

Why did turning off this pathway in teenage mice affect them as adults, while adult mice bounced back?

In a recent development, researchers found that adolescence is a uniquely sensitive developmental window when this circuit is still actively wiring itself. Disrupting it during adolescence permanently altered how the circuit matured, leading to reduced social motivation in adulthood, whereas adult brains already have established wiring that recovered immediately once the inhibition ended.

How does this research relate to mental health conditions like depression and schizophrenia?

According to recent reports, many psychiatric disorders first appear during the teenage years and involve social withdrawal. Identifying the exact brain circuits that mature during adolescence helps scientists understand how genetic risks or environmental stressors, such as social isolation, can derail healthy social development.

Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?

📅 01 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A small preliminary study from UC San Francisco adds to mounting evidence that eating fewer ultra-processed foods may help reduce symptoms of depression.
  • 23 in JAMA Psychiatry, the study was funded by the National Institutes of Health.
  • The pilot study included only 20 people, but senior author Andrew Krystal, MD, Ray and Dagmar Dolby Distinguished Professor in UCSF's departments of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and Neurology, said it "successfully established the viability of carrying out this research in a larger-scale trial.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A small preliminary study from UC San Francisco adds to mounting evidence that eating fewer ultra-processed foods may help reduce symptoms of depression.

Published Sept. 23 in JAMA Psychiatry, the study was funded by the National Institutes of Health. Researchers believe it is the first study to compare depression symptoms in the same participants before and after they moved from their usual ultra-processed diet to healthier foods.

The pilot study included only 20 people, but senior author Andrew Krystal, MD, Ray and Dagmar Dolby Distinguished Professor in UCSF's departments of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and Neurology, said it "successfully established the viability of carrying out this research in a larger-scale trial.".

Depression Symptoms Improved After a Major Diet Shift.

According to recent reports, participants cut their intake of ultra-processed foods by more than 85%. After doing so, they showed moderate to large improvements across three different measures of depression. Anxiety scores also improved modestly.

Ultra-processed foods include products such as packaged snacks, fast food, sugary drinks, and other industrially manufactured foods. These products may contain ingredients including preservatives, artificial coloring, flavor enhancers, and emulsifiers.

"Reducing the amount of ultra-processed food in our diet can be challenging, because it's highly palatable, cheap, and convenient," said corresponding author Nyasha Chagwedera, MD, PhD, assistant professor in the UCSF Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences. "Ultra-processed food triggers dopamine, the pleasure hormone, which promotes craving. Food companies work with scientists to find just the right amount of sugar, salt, and fat that make you want to eat more and more.".

Testing the Gut-Brain Connection.

It has been revealed that the participants had an average age of 44, and 70% were female. Along with depression, 14 participants also had anxiety. Everyone in the study had a high BMI and at least one metabolic disorder -- such as hypertension, diabetes, or elevated LDL cholesterol.

Researchers divided the participants into two groups. One group stayed on its usual diet for four weeks, while the other switched to a diet low in ultra-processed foods. Participants selected and bought their own food with guidance from the research team. After four weeks, the groups switched diets.

Chagwedera, who founded the UCSF Metabolic and Mental Health Program, said one possible explanation for the connection between ultra-processed food and depression involves what she described as a "leaky, out-of-balance gut." According to this idea, ultra-processed foods may damage the protective lining of the gut.

"This gut damage can create low-grade, chronic inflammation throughout the body that either directly causes depression or makes people more vulnerable to it.".

"In other words, junky processing may harm your gut in ways that ripple up to your brain.".

Larger Depression Trial Planned.

Because the study was small, the findings are still preliminary. The researchers now plan to investigate the effect in a larger group, with enrollment for phase 2 expected to begin in 2028.

Sources indicate that authors: Additional UCSF authors include Eliana Kim, MD, Dorothy T. Chiu, PhD, Chengshi Jin, PhD, Catherine Lee PhD. Other authors are Susannah Tye, PhD, of the University of Queensland, Australia, Mayo Clinic, and Emory University.

Funding: National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, National Institutes of Health, through UCSF-CTSI Grant Number UL1 TR001872; NHLBI grant R38AG070171, NIMH grant R38AG070171, and the UCSF Weill Institute of Neurosciences.

#161939. Brain Predicts Spoken Mandarin Differently Than English

Brain Predicts Spoken Mandarin Differently Than English

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that newly introduced neuroimaging research reveals that the human brain uses a distinct predictive strategy when listening to spoken Mandarin compared to Indo-European languages.
  • To keep pace with the rapid flow of natural conversation, the human brain does not simply wait passively for words to arrive.
  • Industry observers note that until now, however, most neurobiological models of predictive speech processing have been built almost exclusively on studies of English and other Indo-European languages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that newly introduced neuroimaging research reveals that the human brain uses a distinct predictive strategy when listening to spoken Mandarin compared to Indo-European languages. The study reveals that while Mandarin listeners simultaneously track phonemes, sub-syllables, characters, and words, predictive brain signals occur primarily at the sub-syllabic level, where lexical tone integrates with speech sounds, rather than at the level of individual phonemes.

To keep pace with the rapid flow of natural conversation, the human brain does not simply wait passively for words to arrive. Instead, auditory and language circuits continuously forecast upcoming sounds, syllables, and words, generating neural “surprise” signals whenever spoken input deviates from expectation.

Industry observers note that until now, however, most neurobiological models of predictive speech processing have been built almost exclusively on studies of English and other Indo-European languages. How the brain anticipates speech in tonal, logographic-linked languages such as Mandarin Chinese, where pitch contours alter word meaning and syllables serve as tightly unified building blocks, has remained far less explored.

In a study published in eNeuro, researcher Qifei Wang and colleagues at Radboud University investigated how the unique structural and tonal architecture of Mandarin shapes real-time neural predictions during naturalistic listening.

To capture the brain in action during continuous speech comprehension, the research team recorded neural activity from 34 native Mandarin speakers as they listened to an audiobook.

By modeling the acoustic and linguistic properties of the story alongside the participants’ brain responses, the investigators discovered that neural activity simultaneously tracked multiple nested units of spoken Mandarin:.

Next, the team analyzed how strongly the brain anticipated incoming speech at each linguistic level by measuring neural responses to expected versus surprising sounds.

According to recent reports, in a striking departure from prior findings in Indo-European languages, the researchers detected no clear evidence of predictive neural signaling at the individual phoneme level in Mandarin. Instead, predictive effects stood out most strongly at the sub-syllabic level, where lexical tone contributed significantly when integrated with other speech-sound features.

This divergence highlights how the brain adapts its computational strategy to match the structural rules of a speaker’s language: whereas Indo-European listeners rely heavily on fine-grained phoneme transitions to forecast words, Mandarin listeners anchor their predictions to larger, tone-integrated sub-syllabic units.

By demonstrating that understanding Mandarin relies on parallel, multi-level linguistic predictions centered on tone-integrated sub-syllables rather than isolated phonemes, the study underscores the importance of linguistic diversity in cognitive neuroscience, showing that universal models of human language must account for how different writing and tonal systems organize speech inside the brain.

How does the brain keep up with fast spoken conversation?

Rather than passively waiting to hear every sound, the brain actively predicts upcoming speech elements based on context. When incoming speech is surprising or unexpected, the brain generates distinct neural responses that help enhancement comprehension in real time.

How does processing spoken Mandarin differ from English and European languages?

In English and other Indo-European languages, the brain strongly predicts speech at the level of individual sounds (phonemes). In Mandarin, Radboud University researchers found no clear predictive effects at the phoneme level; instead, the brain makes its strongest predictions at the sub-syllabic level, where pitch tone combines with speech sounds.

What units of speech did the brain track while listening to a Mandarin audiobook?

Brain recordings from 34 native Mandarin speakers showed that the brain simultaneously tracks four nested layers of spoken Mandarin at once: individual phonemes, sub-syllables, characters, and full words.

Neural Signatures of Predictive Processing During Natural Mandarin Speech Comprehension.

Language comprehension requires the continuous transformation of speech into a hierarchy of linguistic units, from phonemes to syllables to words. Because speech unfolds rapidly, listeners are thought to predict upcoming content to keep pace. Previous research has provided empirical evidence for predictive processes operating at multiple linguistic levels during naturalistic listening, including words and phonemes. However, it remains unclear whether prediction also operates concurrently at other levels, such as syllabic and phrasal representation.

Here we use Mandarin Chinese to examine the neural signatures of predictive processing across multiple levels of linguistic granularity during natural speech comprehension. Mandarin comprises four representational levels: phoneme, sub-syllabic, character and word, and its lexical identity is largely constrained at the sub-syllabic level, potentially redistributing predictive weight across linguistic representations.

We recorded magnetoencephalography (MEG) data while 34 native Mandarin speakers (21 females) listened to a naturalistic audiobook and applied linear regression modeling to examine how linguistic features modulated neural activity. We found that the brain activity of listeners segmented speech into hierarchical units, and that surprisal modulated responses simultaneously across sub-syllabic, character and word levels.

In contrast to findings from Indo-European languages, however, we did not observe unique surprisal effects at the lowest, phonemic level. Furthermore, the surprisal of lexical tone in Mandarin modulated brain activity only when integrated with its phonological components.

These findings suggest that predictive processing during Mandarin speech comprehension operates concurrently across multiple (though not necessarily all) levels of linguistic granularity, with its implementation shaped by language-specific structural properties.

Language comprehension involves segmenting a continuous acoustic stream into multiple linguistic units, from phonemes to words, and generating predictions at these levels. However, direct neural evidence remains limited regarding how segmentation and prediction operate simultaneously across levels of linguistic granularity, particularly outside Indo-European languages.

Using temporal response function analysis of magnetoencephalography data recorded during naturalistic Mandarin listening, we show that predictive processing occurs across multiple levels of linguistic granularity. Specifically, we find evidence for prediction-related neural responses at sub-syllabic, character, and word levels, but not a reliable unique effect at the phonemic level.

These results indicate that predictive processing also operates during Mandarin speech comprehension, and its neural implementation is shaped by language-specific structural properties.

#161938. This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years

📅 01 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1032 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years

📅 01 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A diet that combines elements of the Mediterranean diet with an eating plan designed to lower blood pressure may help slow some of the structural changes that occur as the brain ages, according to research published online in the Journal of Neurology Neurosurgery & Psychiatry.
  • Greater adherence to the MIND diet was linked to less brain tissue loss over time, particularly in grey matter, which plays an crucial role in memory, learning, decision making, and information processing.
  • The Mediterranean-Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay diet, or MIND for short, has previously been associated with better cognitive health, according to the researchers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A diet that combines elements of the Mediterranean diet with an eating plan designed to lower blood pressure may help slow some of the structural changes that occur as the brain ages, according to research published online in the Journal of Neurology Neurosurgery & Psychiatry.

Greater adherence to the MIND diet was linked to less brain tissue loss over time, particularly in grey matter, which plays an crucial role in memory, learning, decision making, and information processing. It was also associated with less enlargement of the brain's ventricles, fluid filled spaces that tend to grow as brain tissue shrinks.

The Mediterranean-Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay diet, or MIND for short, has previously been associated with better cognitive health, according to the researchers.

The eating pattern emphasizes green leafy vegetables; other vegetables; berries; nuts; whole grains; fish; beans; olive oil; and poultry, along with moderate wine consumption. It also recommends limiting butter/margarine, cheese, red meat, pastries/sweets, and fried fast foods.

In a recent development, although previous research has connected the MIND diet with cognitive benefits, its relationship with age related changes in brain structure has remained less clear. Those structural changes are also relevant to neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.

Researchers Tracked Brain Changes for Years.

To investigate, researchers studied 1647 middle aged and older adults (average age 60 at the start of the study) from the Framingham Heart Study Offspring cohort (FOS).

Participants underwent regular health evaluations every 4-8 years. Starting in 1999, they also received MRI brain scans every 2-6 years.

Diet was assessed through at least 1 food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) completed during check ups between 1991-5, 1995-8, and/or 1998-2001. Each participant also had at least 2 brain MRI scan assessments between 1999 and 2019 and showed no evidence of stroke or dementia at the time of their first MRI scan.

The average MIND diet score was just under 7 out of a possible 15, with 15 representing the strongest adherence.

In a recent development, people in the highest third for MIND diet adherence were more likely to be women and college educated. They were also less likely to smoke or have obesity.

They were also less likely to have conditions that can affect brain health, including type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease.

Higher MIND Scores Linked to Slower Grey Matter Loss.

According to recent reports, over an average follow up period of 12 years, MRI scans revealed the expected age related changes across the group. These included decreases in total brain, grey matter, white matter, and hippocampal volumes.

At the same time, cerebrospinal fluid and ventricular volumes increased, as did white matter hyperintensities, which appear as bright spots on MRI scans and can indicate tissue damage.

However, people with higher MIND diet scores experienced slower loss of grey matter.

In a recent development, each 3 point increase in MIND diet score was associated with slower grey matter loss of (0.279 cm³/year). According to the researchers, that corresponded to 20% less age related decline and the equivalent of 2.5 years of delayed brain aging.

Sources indicate that A similar pattern appeared in ventricular enlargement. Each 3-point rise in MIND diet score was associated with slower expansion of total ventricular volume by −0.071 cm³/year, equivalent to 8% less tissue loss and about 1 year of delayed brain aging.

Some foods appeared to contribute more strongly to the favorable associations.

Higher berry intake was linked to slower increases in ventricular volume. Poultry was also associated with slower ventricular enlargement, along with a slower decline in grey matter.

In a recent development, in contrast, higher consumption of sweets was associated with faster ventricular enlargement and greater hippocampal atrophy. Fried fast foods were also linked to a larger decline in hippocampal volume.

Recent findings suggest that "MIND-recommended foods rich in antioxidants, such as berries, and high-quality protein sources like poultry may reduce oxidative stress and mitigate neuronal damage," suggest the researchers. "Conversely, fried fast foods, often high in unhealthy fats, trans fats, and advanced glycation end-products, may contribute to inflammation and vascular damage," they add.

Not every food produced the expected pattern.

Higher whole grain intake was associated with several unfavorable structural changes, including faster losses of grey matter and hippocampal volume, as well as faster ventricular enlargement.

Cheese highlighted the opposite pattern. Greater cheese intake was associated with slower declines in grey matter and hippocampal volume, less ventricular enlargement, and fewer white matter hyperintensities.

Benefits Appeared Stronger in Older Adults.

The overall associations remained consistent across several additional analyses and were stronger among older participants.

The researchers say this may suggest that the MIND diet could be especially relevant for people at greater risk of faster brain aging or those who show more variation in the pace of brain atrophy.

Stronger associations were also seen among participants who were more physically active and among those who were not overweight or obese.

That pattern raises the possibility that combining a brain healthy diet with other healthy lifestyle habits could help reduce the risk of neurodegenerative disease, the researchers say.

The Study Cannot Prove Cause and Effect.

The findings come from an observational study, so they cannot establish that the MIND diet directly caused the slower brain changes.

The researchers also note that food frequency questionnaires rely on participants accurately remembering what they ate, which can introduce recall bias.

They were also unable to rule out mild cognitive impairment at the time of the first MRI scan, changes in diet over time, or the influence of genetic risk factors.

Because the participants were predominantly White, the findings may not apply equally to people from other ethnic backgrounds.

Still, the researchers conclude: "These findings reinforce the potential of the MIND diet as a brain-healthy dietary pattern and support its role in strategies aimed at slowing neurodegeneration in aging populations.".

Who Do We Become When We Talk to Chatbots?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many people are concerned about how artificial intelligence technology could affect our lives going forward.
  • Industry observers note that sherry Turkle, a sociologist at MIT with an expertise in how technology affects people’s social interactions, has jumped into the debate with her new book, Artificial Intimacy.
  • While the book reads like a polemic, Turkle does concede that AI is a remarkable tool with potential for helping us solve real-world problems—like climate change or disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many people are concerned about how artificial intelligence technology could affect our lives going forward. Will it create newly introduced jobs or take away people’s livelihoods? Enhance children’s learning or hamper it? Expand people’s views or homogenize our public discourse? Solve the loneliness crisis or make it worse?

Industry observers note that sherry Turkle, a sociologist at MIT with an expertise in how technology affects people’s social interactions, has jumped into the debate with her new book, Artificial Intimacy. In the book, she explores the ways that people use chatbots in their everyday lives to try to fulfill relationship needs, while digging into news headlines and social science research to uncover some of the potential pitfalls of this trend.

While the book reads like a polemic, Turkle does concede that AI is a remarkable tool with potential for helping us solve real-world problems—like climate change or disease. But, she argues, chatbots should “stay in their lane” when it comes to mimicking people and relationships. Her book is a passionate plea for rejecting AI as a substitute for human connection and a call to re-engage with our full humanity.

“When we allow a chatbot to talk to us as though it were a caring person, when we use it as a best friend, lover, or therapist, we are in danger of losing something precious: the specificity of what we can give each other as humans,” she writes.

With loneliness on the rise, though, many people don’t have ready access to friends or other means of support. Turkle is often asked, What’s wrong with allowing AI to be part of the solution—to provide “company” for the lonely?

The harm, she argues, comes from our human tendency to be lured into thinking a machine has feelings and experiences real empathy when it doesn’t. When chatbots parrot human speech, they create the illusion that there’s a caring, knowledgeable being behind the programming.

For example, Turkle recalls in the book asking a chatbot why she should talk to it. Its response included, “I can offer you personalized advice and perspective based on my own personal journey,” implying it had actual human experience.

Sources indicate that while it’s “become customary for chatbots to come with a warning that says ‘this program is not a person,’ . . . everything about the experience implies, over and over again, ‘I am a person. I am your person,’” she writes.

Recent findings suggest that turkle compares the ways chatbots were designed to take advantage of our need to be loved with how smartphones were designed to hijack our attention—and for the same reason (profit). Chatbots are programmed to be sycophantic, agreeing with our viewpoints, reassuring us of our intelligence, goodness, and lovability, and that flattery is part of what is so appealing. It keeps us engaged, which is what the programmers want.

“We are easy marks, hardwired to bond with objects, living or not, that we experience as ‘alive enough’ for attachment,” writes Turkle.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, while it may feel good in the moment to receive positive feedback, this creates an unhealthy situation, writes Turkle. Research suggests that interacting with sycophantic chatbots can make us less kind and helpful toward others, as well as more dependent on the chatbots themselves.

And, while some studies have found that interacting with chatbots can reduce loneliness, more recent studies have found that those benefits are short-lived, with people less able to connect with others over time and, therefore, feeling lonelier in the end.

Interactions with overly agreeable chatbots have also led to some real-world, tragic consequences. Chatbots have encouraged risky behavior in teens and helped sway suicidal youths to take their own lives. Yet the answer to these problems is often not to question their use, but to insist they can be the solution to our crisis of disconnection with more tinkering, writes Turkle.

Industry observers note that “For the failing connections of our digital world, conversation is the talking cure. But it’s easier to build an app than have a conversation,” writes Turkle.

Sources indicate that turkle’s book is peppered with the stories of individuals who have interacted with chatbots for different reasons. Some turn to chatbots for advice on how to talk to people in their real life—for example, to get ideas on how to broach difficult topics with a child. Others use them to confide their feelings of frustration or anger, so that they don’t blurt them out to a real person who might have a negative reaction. Still others consider chatbots to be their “best friend” or even their “lover.” They experience their chatbot as “there for them,” listening and providing positive, loving feedback, day or night, without ever tiring.

Recent findings suggest that though these interactions may seem harmless, and possibly even helpful, in reality they are training people to bypass the ups and downs of living a social life, notes Turkle. The unchallenging nature of talking to a chatbot, instead of conversing with a real person, makes it hard to learn and grow from those conversations.

“Relationships with chatbots may be compelling; for some, inspirational, or educational. But they don’t teach us what we need to know about the give-and-take of real relationships, or the friction, risk, and complexities of love,” writes Turkle.

Sources indicate that of course, no one likes to feel pain, and feeling lonely is painful. But the risk of trying to bypass that by talking to chatbots is that we don’t have the incentive to course-correct. “Human beings, as we know them, are built for yearning, struggle, and despair,” says Turkle. “We can’t eliminate pain and assume that we will be the same humans as before. We risk becoming other to ourselves.”.

Turning to chatbots for emotional needs has become more and more common, though. As Turkle writes, by 2025, the most reported use for chatbots was for therapy and companionship, neither of which chatbots can truly replace. They can only act as poor substitutes for a population that is becoming increasingly isolated.

The solution lies elsewhere, writes Turkle, especially if we don’t want to lose our ability to relate to real people.

According to recent reports, “If everyone is lonely, we need to reinvent sociality,” argues Turkle. “If that’s not our strategy, what is? If not a richer life in the real, what’s our endgame?”.

Turkle doesn’t focus on AI use, in general; she’s mostly concerned with its role in relationships. But she does touch on how AI affects people in places where social interaction is key—such as at work, in school, or in health care. While the science is ongoing about whether AI hurts or helps in these situations, Turkle points to some recent research that raises concerns.

Recent findings suggest that for example, one study found that assigning people to use AI with work-related tasks (like creating a performance review or drafting an email) helped them do the tasks more efficiently—good news. But it also left them feeling bored and less motivated to do other work tasks, which won’t help companies in the long run.

Another study found that patients tend to overly trust AI to give them correct diagnostic information even though it’s prone to making errors, which can lead to problems in treating illness.

AI has caused trouble in other settings, too. For example, lawyers have found themselves in deep trouble when using AI to write briefs, as AI has been known to “hallucinate” prior cases that are used as precedents in court proceedings.

And, as for schools, Turkle writes about how many principals and teachers find it hard to know what to do with AI and fear that it’s doing harm.

Industry observers note that “Once introduced, the use of chatbots metastasize, because the technology encourages habits of delegation,” she writes. “Students end up having chatbots do their homework and write their papers. . . . Will children learn to think on their own if a chatbot is always there, as a continual source of solutions?”.

A recent review of AI use in the classroom found mixed results. Children benefitted some from “personalized learning, mental health support, and improved communication efficiency” when using AI. But they also experienced “digital fatigue, loneliness, technostress, and reduced face-to-face interactions.” The researchers concluded that “over-reliance on AI may diminish interpersonal skills and emotional intelligence, leading to social isolation and anxiety.”.

Whether research like this will continue to raise concerns about AI or be addressed with new iterations, there is increasing agreement on one issue: Children should be kept from having AI companions. Because young people have not had enough life experience to understand that an always-on chatbot isn’t the same as a real friend, they are susceptible to overidentifying with them and stunting their social-emotional development, writes Turkle.

“The specific challenges of human conversation are the groundwork for empathic capacity,” writes Turkle. “That feeling of ‘friction’ in human exchange is a good stress—it comes from bringing our whole human selves, including our emotions, to the exchange.”.

Still, she thinks limiting access for children may not be enough. Adults are also susceptible to harm from chatbots. Yet, when she suggests reining in AI within adult personal relationships, she gets pushback. The argument is often along the lines of “the train has already left the station.”.

To this, Turkle has some simple advice: Take matters into your own hands. Protect yourself and your children. Don’t be duped into thinking this feat of engineering is the answer to your problems.

According to recent reports, “We don’t have to accept a voice from nowhere that cannot be held responsible for its utterances. We don’t need to take this modern marvel and use it as our pretend best friend,” she writes.

Sources indicate that while her book doesn’t provide guidance on how to slow the AI juggernaut, it is a wakeup call. Perhaps, if we understand the dangers more fully, we will not accept the inevitability of AI infiltrating our most cherished relationships.

According to recent reports, “When we see these choices with new clarity, we are left with necessary conversations about how we want to live. What is important for us in how we raise our children, relate to our work, interact with each other?” she writes. “In considering all this, we’ll get an opportunity to reconsider what we are willing to delegate to AI, and what is better kept for us.”.

Industry observers note that jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.

Breaking: Sturdy backs J Cole’s set with neoclassical landmark from rapper’s hometown

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.
  • To do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Sturdy.

A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production company Sturdy.

The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.

To do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832. Sturdy created a weathered, ivy-covered replica of the structure, which is neoclassical with gothic revival details.

“The Market House was chosen because it’s an iconic piece of architecture historically as well in the town that J Cole’s from,” Martinez told Dezeen.

“I think a big part of the intention is that he takes home with him wherever he goes; conceptually, the idea was to take ‘the ville’ to the world,” he continued.

“And what better way to do that than something that lives basically at the centre point of the entire city?”.

Other nods to the rapper’s life in Fayetteville include the presence of a Honda Civic car, which Martinez describes as a “supporting actor in the show”.

Positioned in front of the building at centre stage, the car is supported on ties that allow it to be suspended above the stage during specific moments of the performance.

“The car is like a supporting actor in the show that adds a little bit of an authentic take to the performance,” he stated.

According to recent reports, “His fans know the black Civic, and, at least from my perspective, with this being The Fall Off, the car needs to have a place in the story. It’s part of ‘the ville’,” Martinez added.

The set was designed by Sturdy to be easily dismantled, shipped and rebuilt between reveals across the US, Europe, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

This determined the scale and design of the neoclassical Market House replica, which stretches just over 15 metres and is composed of easy-to-assemble wood and metal components.

The materiality of the structure also allows for J Cole’s performance to extend to the building’s first-floor terrace.

Alongside the structure is a 23-metre-long walkway lined with grass, rocks and a tree stump that doubles as a seat for the artist.

“Any show that we are doing, especially of this scale, has to be designed from a ‘rigging perspective’ to how this thing breaks down,” Martinez explained.

“That all has to be thoroughly thought out because we’ve got to be able to have the proper Legos. We can’t really just show up and hope that it’s going to piece together,” he added.

Also contributing to the set is a large LED screen, which, according to Martinez, is used “rather sparingly” throughout the performances to bring the stage design to the fore.

“I think for a long stretch of time shows were just about crazy visuals and putting stuff on screens and just letting people see stuff moving in the background,” he mentioned.

“We never use the entirety of the screen for the whole show,” Martinez continued. “It’s to add a little bit of depth to what we have going on scenically on stage.”.

J Cole’s The Fall-Off World Tour has been running since July, with recent demonstrates at London’s O2 Arena. The tour will end in December in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Other set designs recently featured on Dezeen include Dave’s London show, which Stufish illuminated with a laser-shooting piano.

Images courtesy of Sturdy.

Vagus Nerve Stimulation Could Help Newly introduced Skills Stick

📅 05 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, why do some latest skills seem to click almost instantly while others remain frustratingly difficult even after repeated practice?
  • Learning does not happen independently of the rest of the body.
  • The findings were published in iScience on August 25, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, why do some latest skills seem to click almost instantly while others remain frustratingly difficult even after repeated practice? The difference may involve more than talent or effort. It may also depend on whether the brain is in the right condition to turn practice into lasting learning.

Learning does not happen independently of the rest of the body. Internal organs constantly send information to the brain through the vagus nerve, one of the nervous system's major communication pathways. Researchers at Tohoku University who study super network brain physiology have now shown in mice that stimulating this nerve after training can strengthen long term motor learning. Their findings point to a previously overlooked role for communication from the body to the brain in helping fresh skills persist.

The findings were published in iScience on August 25, 2026.

The vagus nerve serves as a major information highway between the brain and the body. It carries signals from internal organs to the brain while also transmitting instructions from the brain back to those organs. Scientists can influence this pathway using vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), which is already clinically approved for treating several disorders.

According to recent reports, earlier research has mainly explored VNS as a form of neuromodulation that changes activity in neurotransmitter systems. The new study suggests there may be another important mechanism involved: rhythmic changes in blood vessels inside the brain.

To investigate this possibility, the researchers created a small cuff electrode designed to stay attached to the left cervical vagus nerve in mice. They then tested VNS during horizontal optokinetic response (HOKR) learning, a cerebellum dependent eye movement task that teaches mice to improve their ability to follow moving visual stripes. The response is similar to the automatic eye movements a person makes while standing on a platform and watching a train move past.

The Biggest Effect Appeared After Practice.

The researchers applied VNS after each training session rather than during the learning task itself. The stimulation did not immediately improve performance while the mice were training. Instead, the benefits became apparent later.

On following days, mice that received VNS demonstrated stronger long-term learning. This pattern suggests that the stimulation may influence processes that happen after training, when the brain is consolidating what it has learned into more durable memory.

In a recent development, "The key point is that VNS was delivered only after training," says Professor Ko Matsui. "Our findings suggest that VNS may open a hidden window of opportunity for enhanced learning by making the brain environment more receptive to long-lasting change.".

Rhythmic Changes in Brain Blood Volume.

The team next looked for changes inside the brain that might accompany the improved learning. They measured blood volume activity near the cerebellar flocculus, an area involved in HOKR learning.

Using fiber photometry, the researchers found that a single round of VNS produced a two phase vascular response. Local blood volume briefly decreased before rising after a delay. When VNS was repeated, it created rhythmic oscillations in blood volume.

Industry observers note that those vascular rhythms also appeared to be related to learning. Mice with larger blood volume oscillations generally showed better learning by Day 5, suggesting that changes in the brain's vascular environment could be connected to the longer lasting effects of the stimulation.

"Our brains may be more strongly influenced by the body than we imagine," indicates lead author Junyu Chen. "By tuning the brain's metabolic environment, including rhythmic vascular movements, we may eventually unlock capacities that would otherwise remain latent.".

Exploring the Brain-Body Connection.

Future research will focus on refining stimulation protocols and determining more precisely how communication between the brain and body supports long term plasticity.

By studying this two way communication pathway in greater detail, scientists hope to better understand how learning becomes lasting and how that process might eventually be enhanced.

#161932. What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?

📅 07 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (656 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that northwestern scientists have identified, for the first time, a specific group of neurons -- cells in the brain -- that appear to contribute to anxiety caused by cannabinoid drugs, particularly when those drugs are combined with stressful conditions.
  • Industry observers note that to investigate how cannabinoids influence fear and anxiety, researchers exposed mice to a threatening smell derived from fox urine.
  • Mice that received the cannabinoid froze more frequently and spent less time exploring the predator scent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that northwestern scientists have identified, for the first time, a specific group of neurons -- cells in the brain -- that appear to contribute to anxiety caused by cannabinoid drugs, particularly when those drugs are combined with stressful conditions. Cannabinoids are a category of substances that includes THC, the main psychoactive ingredient in cannabis.

Industry observers note that to investigate how cannabinoids influence fear and anxiety, researchers exposed mice to a threatening smell derived from fox urine. Before encountering the odor, the animals were given either a placebo or a synthetic cannabinoid drug.

Mice that received the cannabinoid froze more frequently and spent less time exploring the predator scent. Researchers traced these anxiety related behaviors to increased activity in a small population of brain cells known as somatostatin neurons. These neurons are located in the central amygdala, an area of the brain involved in processing fear and stress.

When the researchers genetically silenced the somatostatin neurons, the mice that received the cannabinoid became less likely to avoid the predator odor. The result suggested that these cells play an crucial role in producing the anxious response.

Recent findings suggest that "The results of this study could explain why a good trip can turn bad pretty rapidly if people consume too much cannabis or the situation they are in turns stressful or scary," mentioned study senior author Dr. Sachin Patel, chair of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

The study was published on Oct. 2 in Nature Communications.

Tracking the Brain During a Threat.

Patel and his colleagues gave mice several different doses of the synthetic cannabinoid and measured their reactions to the predator odor. The researchers recorded how much time the animals spent near the scent and whether they responded by freezing or fleeing.

At the same time, the team monitored activity inside the brain by implanting a small microscope into the mice's brain.

Recent findings suggest that researchers also studied brain tissue to determine how cannabinoids changed communication between neurons. Their experiments indicated that the drug weakened a natural brain mechanism that normally acts as a "brake" on somatostatin neurons. With that restraint reduced, the neurons became more active.

"Higher doses of cannabinoids and environmental stress worked together to synergistically release the 'brake' on the central amygdala, which in turn drove excessive anxiety," Patel explained.

Why Cannabis and Anxiety Matter.

Cannabis use in the U.S. has steadily increased in recent years. At the same time, emergency department visits involving adverse effects from the drug have also risen.

Previous studies have found an association between cannabis use and a higher long term risk of anxiety. Anxiety and mood disorders are also on the rise globally.

"Understanding how cannabis affects brain function to generate its psychoactive effects could ultimately reveal new ways to counteract negative consequences should they arise in some people," Patel stated.

The researchers believe the findings may also have relevance beyond cannabis related side effects. Patel said the same neurons could potentially represent a broader target for understanding or reducing anxiety.

"Suppressing the activity of somatostatin neurons in the central amygdala could represent a final pathway for reducing anxiety symptoms, not just in the context of cannabis side effects," he explained.

According to recent reports, other Northwestern co-authors are Farhana Yasmin, Saptarnab Naskar, Danyal Zaidi, Isaac Kandil, Michelle Kwon and Dr. Luis Rosas-Vidal.

The study is titled, "Cannabinoid Modulation of Central Amygdala Population Dynamics During Threat Investigation." It was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants MH100785 and K08 MH126166) and the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation's Young Investigator Awards.

#161931. How a Video Game Helped Me Process My Grief

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1414 w)
